But do be wise, especially if the machine had been put aside through winter, and take the trip leisurely. Your daily mileage will depend absolutely on your degree of fitness, but person- ally I think a hundred is on the long side. At ten miles an hour (whieh is above the all-in touring average) you have to be ten hours in the. saddle. This is a bit too much for most people. Before starting on a pleasure tour I always spend an afternoon overhauling the machine. Every nut and bolt is tightened, chain adjusted just right, lubrication attended to at-every point, patches on tubes examined, and covers given a run over for outward and visible and inward and (almost) invisible signs of trouble. The brakes, too, are carefully readjusted and the shoe-blocks examined for wear. Lamps are taken off, thoroughly cleaned, and refilled. One word of warning. When you are studying out your route, find out beforehand the lightin' regulations of the counties you pass through. You don't want your tour to end in a trip to the Police Court.

Light Sidecar Vibration. This note is really intended for users of feather weight sidecars attacb.ed to a single sylin.ler motor cycle; not so much ter Ihose who possess a heavy combination connected With a poweriul machine. Few riders seem to appreciate to the full the evil influences of vibration, and seldom take any steps to ream:Oil:it as much as possible. The vibration from the engine passes through the light side car chassis,. with the result that coupling's tend to shake loose. For this reason it is essential to examine the machine at regu- lar intervals. A rattle usually indicates that something is coming loose, and failure to attend to it may cause an accident. The vibration is increased if the side car is run empty. To overcome this difficulty stray down the spring 4 of the side car to the chassis so that they are always under slight tension. This is done with a well-sprung perambulator. •It answers equally well with side cars. The ,medguard has a way of ;working loose; hence this part should be: examined at the• same time as the couplings are under inspection.

Lubricating the Springs. In the early days of motoring very little at- tention was bestowed upon the important ques- tion of spring lubricating.. But it was soon realised that it was a subject derda'nding, close attention, since upon it depends in a very large measure the comfort of .the driver and passen- gers. At the sarat,time, many motorists are very careless in this respect, and it is quite a common sight to see 'rust oozing out from be- tween the leaves after heavy rain. Some motor cars might also be devoid of springs, .the result of inattention to their lubrication. It com- paratively simple matter to insert some suitable lubricant between the leaves of the springs, when the improvement in running is im- mediately noticeable. Although we are justi- fiably proud of our English roads they are far from perfect. This is particularly the case at the present moment, since never before have our highways been used so much or for such ,heavy traffic as they have during the last six months. Good springing is therefore indispensable. Ann good springing implies lubrication. The latest device in this connection hails from America, and takes the form of a separate oil cushion tc be inserted between the leaves. The cushion is simply a perforated strip of steel with the holes filled with suitable lubricant and covered with a thin membrane to facilitate transport. When in the spring the latter mixes with the lubri- cant, which retains its ,effectiveness a very con- siderable time.

The Budget. ' From the motorist's point of view the Budget introduced by Mr. McKenna last week is a juFA, one. There have been many. rumours of late concerning_ the future taxation of this vastly important industry, nearly alt of which, as usually happens, have proved to be wrong. Perhaps the best feature of the Budget is the encouragement it gives to the building of light ears, which are comparatively inexpensive to buy, and cheap to run. The heavy car, with its huge petrol consumption and its rapid wear upon thityres, will soon, become a.thing of th: past save for those whose means are practically unlimited. The,,effect of the new taxation shOuld certainly prove to be a great. benefit to home industry. Foreign cars which attraet so many people because of their apparently low price will suffer greatly, since they are all rated It such a high horse-power. Even the Ford Iwner will be called upon to pay £lB 18s. Pur- lhasers will in future greatly favour the home -lroduced light car. The sixpenny tax on petrol tuts not been increased, so that there is no ex- -mse whatever for the present iniquitious prices 'hat are being charged.

div.head: EX JOTTINGS BY AN tux JOURNALIST.
div.p: THE EX JOTTINGS BY AN tux JOURNALIST.

Creditable Public Service. At last week's • meeting • we.: were reminded that Mr. A. J. Jolley has completed four-and; twenty years' membership of the Board of Guardians. That is very good indeed, but of course it by no means constitutes a record. I have attended the meetings of at least two similar bodies having several members with the like term of service, and one of them had actually doubled it.

Long Pastorates. The district in which I met the. fifty-year- service Guardian was likewise remarkable for the extreme length of its ministerial periods of service. Omitting the Anglican clergy for obvious reasons—though, with a solitary exception, these had held their livings without change to well into the second generation—there were in that part of the country pastors of Baptist churches who had occupied the same pulpits over 40, 37, 35, 22', 21 and 18 years respectively, and Congregationalist ministers who had served their 4,people. for 30, 24 and 22 years. The onl, 4v41:0 spent the shortest time,there'.came from a'village within the area over which this paper circulates. Bairns' Hymns.

, a bairns' hymn", was the dying request of an eminent Scottish divine, and 1 have often wondered with what sort of selec- tion his friends complied. "Foyer's" antici- pation of the revue chorus with the expression "Oh, let us be joyful," brought to my mind several hymns sung in Sunday school when I was ari infant scholar. Naturally the one that camo uppermost was— " Here we suffer grief and pain, Here we meet to part again; In heaven we part no more— Oh, that will be joyful," de.

Fancy, setting healthy kiddies to sing in that strain yet, so far as my, recollection goes, the hymns were mostly like unto the one just quoted—" There is a land of puredelight," "I want to be an angel," "We sing of the realms of the blest ' . . . what must it be to be there?" There is a heppy land, fel-, far akk-ay," Ste., dm. Unsuitable as they were at the time, for upwirds of half-a-century they have stuck in my memory; so that, my story has its moral. "The Strain Is Too Much."

In last week's "Stage and Kinema" column I read how, for the above reason, Mr. Norris is unable to play "John Glayde" more than one night a week. Similarly, the late Miss Heath (Mrs. Wilson Barrett) was an exceedingly con- scientious actress, and "East Lynne" was her "nervy" night. Accustomed to put her whole soul into whatever she undertook, Miss Heath in this surpassed her normal self, playing the exacting part with such earnestness and inten- sity that she was generally ill after the per- formance. No doubt many of my older readers saw her in it in their youth—say, some 40 years ago. "Too Much."

As for those who flocked to witness the un- rivalled performance in the town in which I then dwelt—well, the aged cloak-room attend- ant at. the theatre solemnly and in-all apparent sincerity confided to me that whenever "East Lynne" was billed the ladies went amply pro- vided with reserves in the shape of pocket handkerchiefs! This I may in a measure con- firm from .my own experience. "East Lynne" was nothing at all in. my Way; but when .n young lady relative, rejoicing in ,the possession of a. pass for two—and boxes at that—made it plain that she had counted on my readiness to act as escortn need hardly add that there was no alternative. And, as the flippant song bath it, "We did enjoy ourselves, you bet."- In the midst of one of the most pathetic scenes, when I was doing my utmost 'to suppress a rising in my throat :which I felt to be inconsistent with manliness, my companion turned to me not _merely a tear-dimmed eye, but 'an excessively swollen countenance, and, holding thereto a delicate lace handkerchief whicK /, could not .help reflecting might t4ere and then kxy.p Ikth vigorously wrung with advantage,' hYste*ally sobbed, "Is-is-isn't it nice?" (boo-hoo. To have avowed my candid sentiments would have been not only ungallant but cruel, so I. re- strained myself andsmurmilred quite gently in 'response. "Well—er—for thoee .who like this sort of thirig,—why, of course.this is the sort of thing they like." For my pains I was informed that I was •"a•brute," "a heartless monster," and sundry and divers other smooth and plea- sant things were spoken of and to me. Oh, womnan! *Uncertain, coy, and hard to please, indeed. -Deadheads.

The restriction of the free list so far as the Corporation tramcars and 'buses are concerned set me thinking of this subject in general. The term primarily belongs to the stage, and I remember the composer of "Pierrot and Pierrette," who had good means of observation at "His Majesty's Theatre," strongly deprecat- ing the custom as to "paper" and denouncing the deadhead. He declared that every one who could well afford to buy a paltry Is. seat did not for a moment scruple to ask him to send them tickets. "Yet," he continued, "I know that these same folk would come forward rather generously if I should need some finan- cial aid, or if I wanted (perish the thought!) to borrow a trifle! It is only a custom, and a custom- which must go before the solid com- mon-sense of the British people. At least, for this I hope." Free Joy Rides. _

If my experience goes for anything this same -spirit abounds everywhere, and is by no means confined to theatre-goers—though as to the latter class, the interested reader may bear in mind my own confession respecting "East ,Lynne." In one place where I used to live, a jolly old clergyman would perch on my table, and, swinging his legs, would say, "If I were in your position, I'd travel all over the world and it shouldn't cost me a penny." I was aware that he had already contrived a Trans- atlantic trip by acting as chaplain on an emigrant ship, but soon. afterwards he "went one than that. He secured a berth. to Canada and back by obp4ning reappointment as chaplain for the: -voyage, but some time before sailing • he got free passes•-over the three great Canadian railway systems on the representation that he Contemplated a series of newspaper articles describing his travels. I saw only the introductory column—it appeared in the paper of-Which I was editor;' the others failed to materialise! I know of others who, having to arrange big excursions for their fellow-workers, have from time to time man- aged to "do themselves . well" beforehand as .the guests. of the railway company desirous of catering for the trip. • - . • .. Another Class. •

Then there are those who, if they possibly Can, Will -slip into an agricultural or How& show, or .a band performance or other open- air entertainment, without paying, even though the entrance fee may be quite small. If it be a con- cert, and they are surprised hanging about outside within earshot, the excuse usually is that it is a ease in which "distance lends enchantment." .1 had a friend whO gave Sunday evening organ recitals 'which attracted music-lovers from many other places- of -worship--until. he rather reluctantly adopted my Suggestion that a re- tiring collection ;slsould, be .instituted. for the, reedy organ fund., Then-0, what a fall was there, 'my countrymen !

Millionaire-Smugglers. as a NeW York correspondent pointed out a while ago, there is the anxiety of the Ameri- can citizen to defy ,payment of the dhty pro- vided under the 'Thrill Law.. One day it is a society. woman who conceals pearls in the ample recesses of a ,Gainsborough hat; on an- other, it is a millionaire yaehtsman,"who .for gets to declare ten new suits of clothes made by a Louden tailor; and then came the arrest of an American "Candy King" on a charge of -smuggling dutiable goods 'When the'.CustemS officers asked him if he was quite sUre•he had declared everything, he stoutly,maintained that he had; but, on inviting him to take off his coat, they found that he was wearing two gold watches, and a pearl necklace was round his waist, while his wife was concealing under her blouse a chamois bag Containing two necklaces and a rope of pearls. I fear it must be con- fessed that, when an opportunity for any form ,of "deadheadism" presents there is none righteous; no, not one

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.

Easter in the New Forest. Last week I recommended the Isle of Wight - as a delightful spot in which to spend the Easter holiday. If time allows the New Forest should be included in the trip, the two Conibined mak- ing one of the most charming cycling tours imaginable. If this plan is followed the boat should be taken from Ryde to Portsmouth, and the road via Fareham, Botley and Romsey fol- lowed, at which place the route described belos- is joined. The distance from Portsmouth to Romsey is 31 miles. In normal times there is a boat service six times daily between Yarmouth and Lymington, but I understand this is now suspended. Those who are not combining the two tours should start from Winchester and proceed as follows :—Winchester to Romsey, 10.14 Totton, 61; Lyndhurst, 5; Lymington, 81; Bournemouth, 16; Poole, 51; Ringwood, 13; Romsey, 174; Winchester, 10.1.; total 93 miles. The New Forest, covering nearly 100,000 acres, is of surpassing beauty. There is nothing 0191 like it in England. It contains many birds. insects and flowers found nowhere else. Its ponies are noted the world over. The roads throughout the forest are excellent, and mud is almost unknown. Winchester is a fascinatinz, town. It was the capital of Wessex in the 6th century. Its cathedral was started in 635; King. Alfred held his Witan here, and Athelstan created six mints. Winchester College claims to be the oldest public school in Great Britain, although the claim is disputed by the Cathedral School at Canterbury. A day can profitably be spent in sight-seeing. At Romsey. on the Test, a celebrated fishing stream, there is a wonderful Abbey founded by Edward the Elder, son of Alfred the Great in 910, but largely rebuilt in 1125. It contains the finest specimen of Norman work in the kingdom. A little beyond Totton the forest is entered. awl a charming run ensues via Lyndhurst (in the Church there is the celebrated Leighton's fresco), Brockenhurst (so loved by artists) and Lytoingt?..P, whence the Isle of Wight is easily seen. Four miles after leaving Lymington Downton is reached, the site of a Saxon Church, while just to the left is Milford-on-Sea, a Roman camp ,withlsonie yeti' fine cliffs, abounding in fossils. Bournemouth, beautifully situated among the pine, trees, needs no description. Poole, a famous yachtsmen's rendezvous, was a Roman station, and played an important part in Canute's invasion. Its charter was granted in 1248 and Charles 11. made his headquarters during the plague. Ringwood is beautifully situated on the western extremity of the forest, and possesses some charming views and excellent fishing. A magnificent run now ensues to Romsev, passing en route, Picket Post. Stony Cross, and Malwogd House, the home of the ITarcourts. to the left of which there is an old castle, while a quarter of a mile away there is a track leading down to the Rufus Stone, the scene of William 1.1.'s death. The same road is followed between Romsey and Winchester as on the outward journey.

Easter Touring Hints. If for motives of economy alone, more people than ever will spend the Easter holidays awheel this year and, given fine weather, the roads should be teeming with cycles. Of course, a cycling holiday is the cheapest jaunt one may have, and compared with any other form is in- finitely more enjoyable provided one Lakes things leisurely, chooses an attractive route and has a kindred spirit or spirits for companionship.

div.head: ;ATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1916. A FIFTH SHARE.
div.p: ;ATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1916. A FIFTH SHARE.
Labour's Part In The War Pensions Committee.
TRADES COUNCIL PLEASED

The Trades and Labour Council is more 'gratified over the prospect of Labour 'repre- sentation on the Naval and Military War Pensions Committee than with that on the Recruiting Tribunal. Mr. Charles Dukes, secretary of the Council? said so at a meeting of the Trades and Laboull Connell on Tuesday evening, when he reported that on Friday the Trade Union secretaries met at the Town Hall at the invitation of the Mayor (Alderman P. Peacock), who said the committee would probably consist of 21 members representing the Military, the Navy, the Soldiers and Sailors Families' Association, philanthropic societies: and the Town Council. It was agreed by the Mayor that Labour should have a representation of a fifth of the number of the committee, and the general view put for- ward by the Mayor and Alderman James Evans was that the Trade Union secretaries ,present jhould'nominate'friim that meeting a numbekt of -inen from whom the Town Council should el4t But he (Mr. Dukes) opposed that view, showing that it was a violation of the idea of Labour representation if they were not. allowed to ehOose who should represent Uien EirentuallY, the Mayor and Alderman James Evans agreed with the reasonableness of this claim, and it was decided to nominate six names and then vote upon them. If one-fifth of the committee num- bered four, then those who were in the first four in the voting list would be recommended for the committee by the Mayor. If five or six were a fifth of the committee then the others would be recommended for inclusion. The voting was as follows :—Messrs. Dukes, 26; Plinston, 21 Baker, 19; Seabury, 16; Hodson, 13; IRoole, 11.

' The Chairmen (Mr. Edwin Plinston) told the Council he did not think there would be any difficulty in those names being adopted, and the Secretary added that they would certainly be more representative of labour than the two who had been selected by the Town Council for the Recruiting Tribunal.

div.head: ADOLESCENTS' FRIEND.
div.p: ADOLESCENTS' FRIEND.
Advisoky Committee, To Close Blind- Alley Occupations. •

"There is not a town in England where there is so great a percentage of blind-alley occupa- tions as in Warrington," declared Mr. Charles Dukes at the monthly meeting of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday. Mr. Dukes was submitting his report of the Advisory Trade Committee with the Labour Exchanges for Liverpool and district, and Said they had decided that the Board of Trade should be requested to establish a Juvenile Employ- ment Committee in Warrington, no action hav- ing been apparently taken regarding the reso- lution of the original Advisory 'Trade Com- mittee passed at a meeting held in 1912. Ur. Dukes . expressed the opinion that the committee ought to have been appointed long ago. Everyone was concerned with the difficulties, of blind-alley occupations and the apprenticeship question. Parents were very much worried at present over apprenticeships, as it was most difficult to maintain their chil- dren on the ridiculous Wage received while :learning a craft or trade. There were' many difficulties in this respeet-in our local industries,' and he thought the committee which was to be appointed would be most useful. The Chairman (Mr. Edward Plinston) recalled that early in 1913 a sub-committee was ap- pointed by the Education Authority to meet for the purpose of organising a Juvenile Advisory Committee to deal with the question of child labour, but it had fallen through. He was glad pressure was to be brought to bear for the formation of a committee.

div.head: DESPERATE', GERMANS.
div.p: DESPERATE', GERMANS.
Will An Invasion Of England Be Attempted?
",The Tithes" military cOrresponden.t says:—

The Germans have not had the wit to -make the racist of their successes to secure a favour- able peace. Military pride, of -course, was the obstacle, as it always will be. It does not matter to .us. In other recent wars we have seen the high tide of invasion followed by a period of slack water before the tide began to recede. That period we:appear again to have reached, and it is marked by the fact that.the Germans are not now able to deliver a success- ful general offensive in the West, nor to recom- mence operation in Russia without unduly weakening themselves on our own or upon the Italian front.

The German situation needs a desperate remedy, and this may be sought either by an attack upon us in France and Flanders, or by the attempted invasion of the British Isles. We must suppose that there may be an aggregate of 800,000 Germans against our troops in the North, including army troops, heavy guns and cavalry, and that, in addition, the field depots to make good losses are full up., It is, in this event, not an impossible contingency that we may yet be attacked, while, before we can ourselves attack such numbers with success; we must have Tull effectives and more divisions.

The writer has never regarded an attack us at home as impossible. Since Lord French was given the command at home, olr ehaniic arrangements have been reqtored to .hettAr order; . but, taking our .naval and military pre. parations together, and considering the absdute necsssity. for Germany to aim a blow at us, it cannot be said that all risk of an attack upon us has been removed.

div.head: POULTRY FOR PROFIT.
div.p: POULTRY FOR PROFIT.
THE VALUES OF FOODS.

• Every poultry keeper should know something of the relative feeding of certain cereals as well as their suitability ,for various purposes. Maize,, the most popular poultry -grain-with many, un,„ sophisticated poultry - keePers, is decidedly use. fill in its place, but is not of a suitable charac- ter to give fowls in .a small run... For farm poultry - in winter it has no superior, and pos- sibly, during cold weather, a little may be, mixed with other grains for birds in somewhat exposed confined pens; but the backyarder can have little use for maize, which is of too oily and heating a character for the conditions under which his fowls are kept. Barley is another grain that small poultry keepers can dispense with on account of its heating nature, although in very cold weather a proportion of not more than half may be given with other grains for a change. Oats in the absence of wheat, mak.) the most useful staple grain for the poultry keeper, but so many light samples are sold that buyers should stipulate for a good plump wbite oat and see that they get it. In many places oats can be purchased with the ends clipped ' off, and these, though more expensive, are natur- ally of greater feeding value. Dan is useful fox Ei-514t1,1;-;ind'So aoiirhite,,Panadian peas, the latter and buckwheat -loping 'specially useful in winter. It is highly desirable to give the birds , a change of food, for when kept upon one grain entirely *hey become somewhat! stale. T,,iap honsehold sq4s.cettaipili.provide some varietY, but if a. few changes are thade'ainong wheat (if cheap enough), oats, dari, buckwheat and peas the birds will appreciate them.

div.head: NEED OF GREEN FOOD.
div.p: THE NEED OF GREEN FOOD.

A very important item for fowls kept in close confinement is that generally known as green food, which comprises uncooked vegetables, roots, or even grass. When one has a garden a supply of cabbage or lettuce leaves sufficient to last a small flock of birds all the iear round, can generally be obtained, and some keen poultry keepers sow a small patch of rye, to. be cut for the fowls in the early spring, when there is ,very little green food of other kinds. In summer-it is a comparatively simple matter to

obtain an ample quantity of green stuff, for if everything fails some young grass - can.. gathered for the purpose, ad we know some people who give their fowls the lawn mowings. But in winter there is often a rf3al difficulty, and the best plan when there IS nothing else avail- able is to use swede turnips. Mange's, we find. are more likely to cause scouring, but swedes 4?1385!5,8-E-onle es, the neces-, :iseiy Vegetable -r mitt slid afl thtt Yii/V;'h has do is to cut them jn two and hang them on the wire netting within reach of the birds, when they will peek out the inside and leave-the skin like a shell. IP-put upon ;the ground the roots are liable to be trodden about in the dirt. Cabbage leaves and other green stuff should be hung up in the sonic, way, though if one possesses a food chopper it may be put through the machine and given to the fowls either separately or with the soft food. it is not necessary to give a greet quantity, though in summer old birds may be given more green stu4f and less corn; but the fowls should have a small amount every day. Birds that run at liberty or in large grass enclosures will find green stuff for themselves, though in the latter case it must be remembered that during the winter, and also in a very dry, hot summer there is no young grow- ing grass obtainable, so -that something shoul I be given to supply the deficiency.—Middlesex, in " Farm and Home."

div.head: LITTLE THINGS THAT COUNT.
div.p: LITTLE THINGS THAT COUNT.

- .Cleanliness.--Fowls require to be kept scrupu- lously. clean .and perfectly free from insects if their, owner wishes-3o obtain the, best results from them. A dust-bath, coMPo;ed of fine dry earth, sand or ashes, should be provided for them, and with this, Nature's own way, they will do much to clear themselves of the pests. The fowls should now and again be well dusted With'insect-Powder and bloc*, .hellehore powder, using one part of the formi.• to foilr .or,fige• cf the latter. Flowers of sulphur is also a grand cleanser of insects, and its effectiveness can be ,improved by, the addition of carbolic. Mix Bofi.c.'of-..<.,arboliellcid, with 71b. of salphur„, and thiS'willinake'oad of the best insect pewderg 'that can be used. Poultry-houses.—These should be provided with plenty of light, and for this purpose a good- sized window should be put in. They should be limewashed.at least twice a year, and if creosote is used instead of liniewaSb red mites will cease to exist in the poultry-houses. The air space of the house Should be sufficient ti ; allow 10 cubic feet for ,each bird. All perches should be made to lift out of slots, in order that the hous•-s may be thoroughly and quickly cleaned. • A dropping .board should be fixed under the perches, and this will tend to keep the litter on the floor of the house clean and dry. A layer of dry mould or fine ashes on the board will act II as a capital deodoriser. All houses should be , well ventilated at the highest part at each end, and so arranged that no draught can touch the birds; , • Begin with a Few.—lt is a. great mistake for a beginner ,to purchase too much stock for a , start.' Half a dozen birds of a good laying strain I wilt be quite stfficient to practise with. If t-lieY thrive and lay well durinegio more can be added• of the Same. The number can be further increased as the poultry-keeper's knowledge increases. 'Small numbers always do: better than one large quantity WgZtvher.' Thre-o, essential points are to keep the birds dry and clean, and to feed them at regillar hour's. Nothing is of greater importance to all kinds of fowls than that they get a continuous supply of clean, fresh water. _ _ _

Don't.. Iceep fowls in damp, draughty houses, nor yet in dirty ones., Don'tkeep fowls on,the wetteit and worSt land you have ; the better it is the better they will do. Don't run -old fowls and chickens together, as the old ones will only knock the youngsters about, and so stunt their growth. Epsom salts occasionally put in, the drinking water or soft'food ben Splendid medicine to keep fowls in health, and alSo assist their laying powers. _ _ _ _

Overfeeding is a very common mistake made by a beginner in the' poultry-keeping line. Poultry should always be kept keen, seratchin4 about, and ready to fly hungrily upon their food.—" The Feathered World."

div.head: PETUNIAS,
div.p: PETUNIAS,

Where large quantities of plants are required for the summer, -deeoration of the garden, petunias may well be given a trial, as few plants are more effective, more especially in a dry season. If the season is wet and dull the plants make too much growth, 'and the flower production is consequently -lessened. They are easily raised from seed, grow very quickly. and bloom very freely. Seeds sown now and placed in a warm greenhouse will soon develop into strong, stocky plants which when hardened off may be planted out by the end of May.

div.head: PURPLE SPROUTING BROCCOLI.
div.p: PURPLE SPROUTING BROCCOLI.

This comes in at a time when Brussels sprouts, cabbages, and the major part of the .white broccolis are going over, and those who want a tender, wholesome vegetable should grow a breadth of it. It is surprising the quantity or shoots that a well-grown plant will carry. These Ahoot 8 should be frequently gathered cind not allowed to run to flower or they are useless. Provided a good strain is grown, few vege- tables can equal the Purple sprouting broccoli for tenderness, while it is always of a beautiful green colour when properly cooked and sent to table.

div.head: CABBAGE SPROUTS.
div.p: CABBAGE SPROUTS.

div.head: PREPARING FOR BATTLE.
div.p: PREPARING FOR BATTLE.
Trades Council On After-The-
War Policy.
FAR-SEEING EMPLOYERS.'

Declaring that emplcryers have been a little ' more, , far-seeing .than workmen, Mr. Charles 'Dukes, secretary, at the monthly meeting of the Warrington; Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday, supported the desire -of several other 'Trades ' Councils to call a conference of 'Trade Union" organisations to discuss after-the-war problems. Mr. Dukes said that employers had not allowed the national crisis to obliterate their desire to retain their peculiar 'prerogatives upon our economic system, -and he had . watched with grave concern .the-Meeting together. .of-employers representative of -mations; Of. capital. It had been suggested that an llngineers'-.AssoCiation., controlling 'Z300,00000 capital, should be formed ready- for after the war, and the Employers' Parliamentary Association was already working towards their own ends. Neither were Chambers of Commerce letting things slide.

div.head: LABOUR ORGANISATION WEAKNESS.
div.p: LABOUR ORGANISATION WEAKNESS.

With all those facts before them, it made them wonder what sort of a Labour organisation would be able to hold its own. It was time that they commenced to look for. a more ethcient organisation of the Labour movement. If it were necessary for employers to take precautions for .the future, how much more necessary was it for Labour, which was the, weaker of the struggling elements in Society? They did not ,know when the end of the war was going to coilae,. but it was certain that the Labour mow.- meat wouldbe nothing like se effective as it was At the 'Commencement—and. he Anew • that they were hopelessly inefficient even then to cope with capital. The great financial burden which this country would have to bear at the end of the war made one ask who was going to shoulder .that burden. They should think on these things. Several members, including the Chairman (Mr. B. Plinston) spoke in favour of supporting the idea of a national ,Conference, and the..reso- lution was passed unanimously.

div.head: Exemption Age Reduced For Period
div.p: Exemption Age Reduced For Period

O-1 The War. '7=o .shire Education Committee considered •Monday•-a;-res.olUtion..fropa the AShton-awler- •Lyne• and 'StockPort Education Sub-committee recommending a reduction hi the age of exemp- tion of school children. The pro- posal was that full time exemption should be granted to a child between 13 and 14 years of age who is being beneficially employed to the satisfaction of the local authority, and who has obtained a certificate of 300 attendances in not more than two schools in each year for five pre- ceding years. Mr. J. Wild read a number of letters from industrial firms ,setting forth the shortage of labour through employes joining the forces. This applied not only to cotton mills but to other manufactories. They only asked for the con- cessions for the period of the war. Mr. G. Rhodes, K.C., spoke against the pro- posal. The Withdrawal of chldreu at such a period of their school career would affect their .whole after-life. if we were to hcld our own in the future as a manufactlrirtgavitian we should give the children all the adv..) tages we could -now.
Canon Grant Bird said that for the short period suggested they ought to g+ve the help asked.

The Chairman (Dr.'llodgsonl said that if they made the concession asked for it woull pre- judicially affect the children. It NViif3 asking them t 6 go back to the bad old days. It surly could not be right for children of thirteen years of age to work from six o'ciock in the morning until 5.30 in the evening in mills and factories. It would, rob children .of. the educatiOn, they had provided' for them n at great difficulty anti great cost. To employ children of immature age would weaken their health, and they would never, recover and get back the .taste for educa- tion
The resolution was adopted by 15 votes to 10.

div.p: CIA DE STRIKERS.
Stern Warning To Be Given By Responsible Unions.
To-morrow at Glaftgow, a meeting of the Executive To-morrow, of the Federation uf Engineering and Shipbuilding Trades will be _ _

Iheid to discuss certain ireporiant questions of policy, especially that dealing with the attitude of the federation towards the notorious Clyde Workers' Committee. I The National Advisory Committee and the 'Clyde Local Advisory Committee on Productions ;of Munitions will be present, and it has been ;sspecially requested 'that :the vvion.s. local union; will ..make themselves responsible for the at- tendance of representatives from their various district committees. The cobt of living and tho `acceleration of production in regara to shipi eon- rstructicrn 'will be among the subjects for dis- qnssion., :Mr. Lyndon Ifaeassey,.K.C., will at on behalf of the government when the latter subject is being di..ccussed. Prom the very best sources I learn (writes a Labour correspondent) that very stern , measures will be taken with the leaders of the Clyde recalcitrants if they do not give guaran- tees for their future good behaviour. They will first of all, be expelled from their respective unions, and ten handed over to the military authorities for the latter to deal with them in any way they may think fit. Responsible trade union leaders bitterly com- plain that whilst they are taking every possible step to maintain trade union conditions and stimulate the Government into conceding in- creases of wages, or else compelling lower freights, which will result in a decided dinilnu- tion of the-cost of living, the ill-ndvised strikes !which have taken -place on 'the Clyde and else- 'where hare seriously handicapped their eflerts.

The Vogue For Ostrich Feathers. _ . 'Ostrich feathers will Probably have an un- precedented vogue this year, and quite a novelty is the set consisting of muff and collar, of these beautiful plumes. Such a set completes a wrap coat most effectively, the high feather collar taking the place of • the silk ruffle. every. description of neckwear is shown in ostrich 'feathers, which are lavishly used by milliners also. , Large picture hats'jnflne tagel straw have long sweeping Plumes, as sole4hut • quite sufficient trimming. A welcome revival is the' dress of white or ivory lace 'for theatre or restaurant wear, and a novel- trimming, beauti- ful 'also, for such a toile4te, is a spray of large poppies made entirely of soft curled ostrich feathers arranged like the petals of the flowers around large centres of pale green stamins. This trimming is laid a little above the hem of the skirt, a flat bow, of broad velvet ribbon match- ing the feathers in colour finishing the spray, the whole giving a rich and artistic effect to an otherwise simple gown. Two poppies ,on the corsage suffice for relief. Marabout is also to be much in evidence, a number of the high enveloping collars being made of it. It is always becoming, but not as-durable as ostrich feather trimming.

.War-time Wedding Gifts. . Wedding gifts, like weddings, have changed iu their character since the war, and one of the most popular presents just now is something old -and quaint,/ hilt not cumbersome. These gifts have one distinct advantage, they cannot be duplicated. A length of old brocade, an old beaded purse .or bag, an antique mirror or ' screen, or a needlework picture have all been chosen lately as wedding presents for various war brides. Antique jewellery forms another popular gift. It is Said that a great 'deal of this-has 'recently found. its way to the markets, and that Americans are'-bnYing largely, not, however, for wedding gifts. Quite an accept- able, present .to a _bride, is an old dark wood knife :trAy, -which. makes ,useful accessory for the 'writing table...,, Antique fans end :pieces .of old real lace make. delightful presents, whilst sets of furs, umbrellas and parasols, ostrich feathers and boas, have been preferred by several practical young women as wedding gifts from parents and relatives.

to find a •better way of making steam useful. At last he .discovered how. steam could Make wheels' turn ,round:'. - His new, steam engine could do the work of hundreds of men. Then other men found new ways of setting the steam to work. One of these wm Henry Bell. He built a boat, and put a steam engine in it. • Steam plays a great part in this war. If we had not pteam our trains would not be able to carry troops and ammunition. All our factories and workshops would be stopped if we had not got steam. In fact, if we had not got steam we would not be able to carry on the war at all. We have read of great heroes like Nelson and Wellington, but we must not for- get men like Watt, Bell and Stephenson. While the former were fighting these men were doing their best to help their fellow-country- men in another way.—Prom your loving niece, MABEL LA.NGLEY, age 12; 178, Padgate-lane- Niece Edna Fellows, 44, Bewsey-road, points out that trains carry our soldiers to the ports and steamers continue the journey to other lands. The bayonets and guns, shells, bullets and bombs:the men tse have all been -made .by the aid .of steam, and fighting would have been very much more difficult if steam had not been used.

Nephew Ernest W. Sankey, 99, Kimberley- street. says, we can have plenty of steam in Britain, where water and coal are so plentiful. Steam aids in transporting men, ammunition and food. "The machinery in the munition works depend on steam, and, without shells, bullets and guns, the soldiers at the Front are dead men, and England will go through ten times worse than r. Belgium got. 7 • • • Niece Lilian Himsworth, 15, Fitzherbert- street, Warrington' (Beamont Council School), writes one ofrhe?r excellent7,letters. She says:--;... Steam' plays a veiy-iimportant' part in this war. Withont steam it yonldtake'a great deal longer to carry Our brave soldiers across to France and elsewhere. Our soldiers would have to march to their starting-place and then to wait until the wind was right to blow tlrm across the Channel. It would be very incon- venient for our sailors also, because they would have to use sails or oars. We ought to be thankful that steam was invented, because we can travel ever so much more quickly. Steam has played an important part in the transport of food. Six., and has enabled all our troops to enjoy their Meals and ;so maintain their stamina to win this war."

Niece, Elsie Johnson, 32.3, Lovely-lane, de- scribes steam as the giant of industry that has done much to spread civilisation. It is used to drive engines for moving machinery, ships, trains, and ,mine. trucks. In this work it has been a great help: during the war, and at the end of the. war it will be said to have been one of the chief driving powers of the 174ited Kingdom.

Niece Eva HaridleY, 17, Collin-street (St.i BarnabaS"•School).--u We are thankful that we possess 'fuel to make the steam to drive our, locomotives, which are carrying different kinds of materials used in. the manufacture of muni- tions. Without • steam our Navy and merchant ships would be useless. They are able now to guard our shores from the enemy, to carry our soldiers and munitions to different partsl of the world, at the same time bringing us provisions and stopping the enemy from getting any?' •

By MARJORIE.
Women Bakers.

Whilst economists - urge the advantag )4 ef home-made bread, trade experts point out that the cost of fuel has to be considered, and that the -kitchen- range is, much more, 'axtravugant than the. scientifically -constructed hot cnambers of the great bakery. That the bread made by amateurs would :be more nourishing. and .whole-. some than the baker's loaf .is -doubted also by the trade. It is at any rate very certain that women will be compelled to make bread Either in the bakeries, or in their own homes, .en account of the shortage of masculine labour. The trade supports a technical school in the Boroirgh, in London, and a class for women is about to be started there. This is quite an innovation, but it is pointed out that with the aid of modern automatic machinery, women are well able to undertake certain stages of the work. In the confectionery departments women have already proved their efficiency. and have taken the places of 'men formerly employed. In .9.c.ot- land women have always worked in the bakeries, and it is possible that they will be permanently employed in other parts of the United Kingdom. Furniture and the War.

The war will probably bring about modifica- tion in the style of furnishing. At present, the houses of the upper middle anti well-to-do classes are, as a rule, suffocatingly crowded with useless and unnecessary furniture. Now that there are not enough servants to dust and clean even what is required, the superfluous will have to be eliminated in furniture as in other things. Kitchens invariably contain numberless utensils and things that are seldom, if ever, re- quired for use, but they have to lie kelit clean and polished, and overcrowded rooms, crammed with knick-knacks, sofas, table-3, and dust-catching draperies, are as unhealthy as they are inartistic. The Japanese go to the other extreme, and a rich man allows only one of his works of art to appear in a living room at a time, so that it should not be overshadowed by others. We on the other hand are pre- possessed with the idea that the more treasures we can crowd into the drawing-room the better,

div.head: Fried Cucumbers.
div.p: Fried Cucumbers.

Peel two large cucumbers, and cut into sec- tions divided into two, taking out the pulp and seeds and allow the cucumber to drain for a couple of hours. Wish, and Cook with Wmorsel of •butter, a little soup, a teaspoonful of 'pounded sugar, with a dash of vinegar, and a pinch of red popper and two onions. A quarter of an hour's cooking will suffice. Then drain the cucumber on a serviette, and before serving up dip each piece in grease and put into a warm frying pan. 'Drain when of a light gold colour, sprinkle With salt, and serve on a napkin with garniture of fried parsley. •

Savoury Cheese Pudding. • In this pudding hard, dry scraps of cheese and some stale pieces of bread may be made into an appetising dish, with the help of one egg and a little milk. Take a teacupful each of grated cheese and breadcrumbe, and season them .with cayenne pepper, dry mustard, and salt. 'Place a teacupful of milk in a saucepan, and in it heat the above ingredients. Then cool a little, and add a beaten egg. Beat the white to a stiff froth, grease a pie-dish, add the beaten egg to the cheese, &c. Pour into the dish. Put a few bits of butter on the top, and hake in a quick oven for 20 minutes. Serve at once.

Simple Living. I am bound to praise simple life, because I live it and find it good. Many persons know the luxury of a skin bath—a plunge in the pool or sea, unhampered by clothing: That is simple life—direct 'contact with things, life ,with false wrappings torn away—the fine house, fine equipage, expensive habits, all cut off. How free one feels, how good the elements taste, how close one gets to them, how they fit one's body and soul; how. good to see the fire•that warms you, or better yet, to cut the wood that feeds the fire that *arms you; to see the spring where the water bubbles that slakes your thirst, and to dip your pail into it; to see the beams that are the stay of your four walls, and the timbers that up- -hold the roof, to be in contact with the sources of your material 'life; to want no extras, nO shields; to find the Air and water exhilarating; to be thrilled by the stars at night; to be elated over a bird's nest—these are rewards of simple , life.—John Burroughs.

Children, Join This Corner!- Enter The Competitions! Write Your Best! Always Be Glad! Uncle Jack, " Examiner," Warrington.
THE EFFECT OF STEAM ON THE WAR.
liY DEAR CHILDREN,-

When Uncle Ned suggested last week that you should write about the effect of steam on the war, I thought the subject would be rather difficult for his little people; and I gather that has proved to be the case, for only a few have tackled the subject. It will be seen that we have something easier this week—also suggested by Uncle Ned—and I hope you will do your best to please him by entering the competition aml making it a great success. The essays that have been sent in this week are good and to the point. and I have had much pleasure in awarding the prize to
Niece Mabel Langley (773), 178, Padgate-lane, who attends Beanlont Council School.

You would see that Uncle Ned. in his letter last week, thought4we might •begin to ,Proniote' members: of the •' Corner, anti call them' "Sergeants," "corporals," and so on, accord- ing to the regularity with which they write to Uncle Jack, or • the number of times they succeed in winning a, prize, or the number of new. members they get for the Corner. Uncle Ned has written me again this week. I sup- pose he noticed that I did not mention it last' week—and he is the most persistent kind of uncle I know! Well; I may say that / agree with the idea of promotion as a reward of merit, but I don't think it quite the thing to call children "Sergeant" and "Corporal." Of, course, Uncle Ned is a soldier at present, and I am not. That is the difference. I am all in favour of everyone' being in a 'fighting humour now, until those rats of civilisation known as Germans have been treated .as a good terrier would treat a common rat; but when they have been given a shaking and beaten,: there will be the peace beyond, and we'shall•want largely to forget the horrid times through which we are now passing. So we will 'have our promotion scheme, but not on a military basis. But what are the names we must use as titles for those we promote? That 'is 'where I want you all to help _me; and, there Will be a prize for the one who sends Me the 'best suggestions for titles.

div.head: PRIZE IN THE LAST WEEK.
div.p: A PRIZE IN THE LAST WEEK.

Uncle Jack was more pleased than he could say when he heard that he had been able to give a prize to a deserving member just as she was leaving school to begin work and so re- signing her membership of the Children's Corner: for we are no longer "children" when we "start work."

The member is Niece Lily Webb, 27 Cath-1 erine-street. She has been one of my best and ' most regular correspondents; many times she nearly won the prize, and I was sorry more than once when I was unable to make the award in her favour. However, Uncle Ned and I decided to give her a special prize last week for the best suggestion for an essay. Soon after this' I received a letter from her saying she was 14 and had left Heathside School, and regretting that she had not been clever enough to win a prize once. But never mind," she added, "I did ray best." And at the time she had won a prize! Was not that strange? I have since received a note from her saying: . "I received your beautiful, prize and I thank you very much for it. .I was so surprised to win .a prize, .but I have 'Uncle Ned to 'thank for it. She adds she., has started at 'Cros- field's. If she 'attends to her work as diligently as she has attended to her Children's Corner pastime, Messrs. Crosfield will find they made a good bargain when they engaged her.

div.head: SEASONABLE MONTHS IN THE YEAR.
div.p: SEASONABLE MONTHS IN THE YEAR.

January brings the snow, Makes our feet and fingers glow. February brings the rain, Thaws the frozen lake again. March brings breezes, loud and 41.111, Stirs the dancing daffodil. April brings the primrose aweet, Scatters daisies at our feet. May brings flocks of pretty lambs, Skipping by our fleeced hands. June brings tulips, lilies, roses, Fills the children's hands with posies. not Jul brings cooling showers, Apricots and gilblowers. August brings the sheaves of corn, Then the harvest home is borne. September brings the pheasant. Then to gather nuts plAasant. October brings the blast, Then the leaves are.whirling fast. November brings the fog, Ptah' GuY Fawkes upon tho December brings the Yuletide goose. And blazing fires and Christmas truce.
ADOPTED FIVE BABIES.

div.head: Jury's Verdict Of " Manslaughter."
div.p: The Jury's Verdict Of " Manslaughter."
INFANTS HANDED OVER OUTSIDE POST OFFICE.

Some startling disclosures of a woman's almost wholesale adoption of babies were made at. an inquest at the Police Station on Tuesday, when the jury returned a verdict of " Manslaughter " against Ellen Goodwin, of 20, Cockhedge-lane, respecting a two-year-old child, of whom she was the foster-mother, _ _

_ Sitting by Mrs. Goodwin (an elderly woman) was her husband, Charles Goodwin, who, as the Coroner Mr. S. Brighouse) remarked, was at one time the leading licensed victualler at Ormskirk, and also held licenses in Warrington and Widnes. Ile is now a labourer at Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd. He was in custody with his wife on a charge of neglecting the dead child. _ _ _

-- Of four children Mrs. Goodwin received from Nurse Rate Maria Pearce, of 20, Laurel-road: 'Fairfield, Liverpool, three have died. She was paid sums of money With each of them—Es each in two cases, n with another, and £lO with the one upon whom the inquest was held. The children were all handed to her by the nurse at varying times in the last three or four veers outside the Warrington General Post office, Bank Quay Station, or at the Central Station, Liverpool. AS recently as last month Mrs. Goodwin went to *London, and at Euston Station received a baby a few weeks' old from another nurse, who gave her £2O. SON OF A BARMAID.

Nurse Pearce—. was -the first witness called. In reply to the Coroner she explained that the deceased child, which had been registered as Charles Goodwin, was really Henry Edge, the illegitimate child of Mary Edge, who was at one, time a barmaid in War- rington, but had gone to live at a Manchester hotel. The child was born at witness's house. The nurse added that she had always known Mrs. Goodwin as Mrs. Spencer, and had corre- sponded with her in that name during the "four business transactions" she had had with her. She got to know Mrs. Goodwin through adver- tising. Regarding one of the children (not the deceased) she had a photograph .Sent her which showed "how well the baby was getting on." She handed the photograph to the Coroner, who remarked, "Yes, it looks a nice child." The Coroner questioned the nurse as to the address of the mother, Mary Edge, and witness said she did not know it. When she left her home after the confinement she promised to write when she reached Manchester, but never did: "This kind of girl never tell us their addresses. Naturally,' they don't like to do. They just pay the money for nursing and then the money for the foster-mother, and don't want to give you their addresses. If you insist they usually give you false ones." NAMED AFTER ITS FATHER. -

The Coroner pointed out that the deceased had been registered as being the sun of Mr. and Mrs. Goodwin, whereupon witness made some interesting revelations. Remarking that she had always known Mrs. Goodwin as Mrs. Spencer, she added that just before the child was born "Mrs. Spencer" wrote telling her that it would be adopted by her "daughter and son-in-law, Mr. and Mrs. Goodwin," and that "if it is a boy they would like it named John Edward and, if it is a girl, it is to be Edith." The nurse told the mother, who insisted on the baby being named "Henry," after its father. The Coroner then read a letter which Nurse Pearce admitted she had written to Mrs. Good- win, in which she stated, "I am expecting to have news to send this month. Re registering, ' let me have the names of parents to be—her name before marriage, his name, and what he does, and I can manage it. Then there will be eno more trouble. Also what -to call the baby, boy or girl." "Outside• the legal point you know this was very wicked," remarked the Coroner to the nurse. _ _

"Mrs. Spencer did not say the baby was for herself," replied the 4urse. The Coroner: You knew the child was illegitimate. Nurse Pearce: I did not tell her to register the baby in that name, but to tell the Registrar that they were adopting it, and not to register it in that name. _ _ _
The Coroner (to Mr. A. Bottomley, registrar, who was sitting in the Court): Isn't there a letter which shows that she herself registered the child P—Yes.

div.head: BABY AND £lO.
div.p: BABY AND £lO.

The Coroner (to the nurse): You gave Mrs. Goodwin £lO and then wiped your hands of the baby. From the material standpoint it followed that the sooner the child died the better it would be It was not as if she were to be paid so much per week. • Witness: As a rule a person only wants a small sum of money. If she had asked for a big sum then I might have been anxious about it. Mr. A. Browne (for the N.S.P.C.C.): When you parted with the child was it in the best of health ?—No, none oft the children were in the best of health.
What was the matter with it?—lt was not up to very much, and I told Mrs. Spencer it would want a lot of care.

Mr. T. S. Steel (for Mr. and Mrs. Goodwin): It was very weakly, but had lived for two years. Would that be about the teething time?—Yes. Inspector G. H. Wainwright, of the N.S.P.C.C., said it was in consequence of receiv- ing an anonymqus letter respecting the nurse child that he visited the home of Mr. and Mrs. Goodwin, which was then at 10, Naylor-street. The house consisted of four rooms and they had three- children of their own. The rooms wero furnished and in a dirty condition. Mrs. Goodwin worked at Mortimer's Tannery, Orford, so that, with her husband's wages, £2 is. sd. was going into the house weekly. The -Inspector said, in reply to Mr. Steel, that Mr. and Mrs. Goodwin had recently removed to Cockhedge-lane, having bought a chippe:l potato business for £7 10s. Replying to Mr. Bottomley, the Inspector said that for a long time Mrs. Goodwin kept on saying that it was her child.
husband she was going for tho babies,' and every 4414 she returned with one he was angry. Sli& always gave bini a sovereign, and he said he would do his best for the children.

The detective produced a picture postcard which, Mrs. Goodwin, in the name of Mrs: 'Spencer had sent to Nurse Pearce. Mrs. Good- win had written it purporting it to be from her daughter-in-law, who was supposed to have:the baby! It declared, "What a. bonny baby he has become! Charlie says-lifo is worth 'living now." 'Henry ScOtson, itourance agent, of 4,'Slater- street, deposed that Mrs. Goodwin had insured Charles (the deceased) and three other children. Her husband was present at the time. ' Dr, Peacocke said that when he was called to the child a few days before its death it had all the appearance of being neglected. The house was in a filthy condition. The child must have been ill for days before he was called in. He ordered it to be removed to the Union In- firmary.

div.head: BABIES ANGER HUSBAND.
div.p: BABIES ANGER HUSBAND.

Detective-Sergeant Reddington said that when he arrested Mrs. Goodwin she volunteered a statement, in which she said the children were usually two or three weeks old when she took to them. A few months ago she noticed an accouchement advertisement in a London news- paper and wrote to the advertiser—a Mrs. Morris—but received no reply. Last month, however, a woman wrote saying that she had been in communication with Mrs. Morris, who said she would pay her expenses if she would go to London to meet her. She went and re- ceived a baby and £2O, the woman saying that the father of it had been killed in the. war. Mrs. Giaodivin told witness that she never told her

div.head: HONEST OR SUSPICIOUS CIRCUMSTANCES?
div.p: HONEST OR SUSPICIOUS CIRCUM- STANCES?

Dr. Binns, who conducted a post-mortem examination, said the body was generally emaciated. It had died from bronchial pneu- monia, accelerated by starvation. Through want -of food it had not had the vitality to ward off the attack. It only weighed um.. whereas the average weight of a child of two years was 321 b.
In reply to Mr. Steel, witness agreed that teething children very often rejected their food, but he added that he was of opinion that this child was emaciated through want of food.

In addressing the jury, the Coroner said they need not trouble about Mr. Goodwin, but in regard to Mrs. Goodwin, were the circumstances suspicious or honest, considering the facts o! her dealings in children?

The juiy consiidered in private or three minutes, and then returned a verdict of "Man- slaughter" against Mrs. Goodwin. To Dr. Binns the Coroner said tliey were alt much obliged for the way he had conducted the post-mortem examination, and the skilful and lucid manner in which he had given his evidence.

div.head: FOSTER-PARENTS BEFORE MAGIS. TRATES.
div.p: FOSTER-PARENTS BEFORE MAGIS- . TRATES.

Ellen Goodwin and Charles Go(dwin, 20. Cockhedge-lane, were before the magistrates on Monday and were remanded for a week on a charge of neglecting the dead child. The Chief Constable said the facts of the case had been emmunicated to the Director of .Public Prosecutions, and it was desirable that another seven (lays' .adjournment should be granted.

div.head: NEGLECTFUL MOTHER.
div.p: NEGLECTFUL MOTHER.
Inquest On Child Who Was
Burned.
CORONER SUGGESTS PROSECUTION

A severe censure was passed on Mrs. Ellen Ashton, of 9, Pierpoint-street, at the inquest on Tuesday on her nine months' old baby, who had died on Sunday in the Infirmary as a re- sult of being burned ,while at home on Friday. Coroner Brighouse told her that if the pollee did not prosecute her they would not be doing their duty. If he were a Magistrate he would fine her the full penalty.. "I think you should hold your finger in the fire for a minute and see . how. you like he .declared

The mother,- ';Vho is the wife of Harry Ashton, a private in the 3/4th South Lancashire Regi- ment, said she left the child tied in a rocking chair whilst she went to a shop: It was in the house by itself, and when she returned its night jacket and vest had been burned. There was a fire in the grate, but no guard. She thought a spark had flown out of the fire and ignited the child's clothes. VALUABLE ASSET LOST.

Witness having stated that she had four other children between four and eight years old, she admitted, in reply to the Coroner, that on Sun- day Detective-Sergeant Summers had called and she was out, baying left two of the children in the house, where there was a fire, but no fender or fireguard. "And this happened after your child haa been burnt !" exclaimed the Coroner, adding that it was most lamentable that children "shourd be burnt to death, more especially at the present time, for the country could not afford to lose the most valuable assets it possessed. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," the foreman remarking that they were of opinion that Mrs. Ashton had been grossly neglectful. As the inquest concluded Mrs. Ashton col- lapsed, and, water being unavailing in rester- ing her, she was carried out of the court.

div.head: WHY ILLOGICAL ENGLAND IS SUCCESSFUL.
div.p: WHY ILLOGICAL ENGLAND IS SUCCESSFUL.

General Boma is as good a business man and statesman as he is a Soldier—and that is the highest praise we can give him. In resist- ing, on behalf of the Government, a resolu- tion having for its Object the ascertaining of information as to the steps to be taken by the British Empire and the Allies with respect to trade conditions after the war, General BOTHA told the South Africa Union House of Assembly on Wednesday that the motion was "premature." We should first, he declared, "devote our attention to giving the Germans a sound hiding. The greatest question with which we can occupy our Minds is the defeat of the, common enemy. After that there will be ample time to deal with the fiscal ques- tion." There is a clearness of perception and a directness of application of essentials and 'fundamentals on the part of BOTHA that re- mind one forcibly of CaostwELL. His reason- ing was successful, for the motion was with- drawn, and South Africa is evidently to pro- ceed, undistracted, upon the laudable path of doing its utmost, to use BaraA's own words, "to assist the British Government to bring the war to ,a successful issue." The success- ful prosecution of the war is, for the moment, all that counts; it is the only thing that will count till the last shot of the conflict has been fired, for unless the Hun has the really good hiding that BOTHA is so anxious to help to administer, there will be an end to permanent peace or successful trading.

It is strange that in this country those aggressive people who want us to lay siege to enemy trade at .once are the very people who desire us, at the same time, to abandon our trade in order to mike a short cut to victory. 'finiversal conscription and ithe aban, -donment of the trade of the country comes as the demand..in one breath; break down .or vapture-thOtindervf the enemy and so cripple him for ever is the urgent advice that comes with the following breath. It is the indecent haste of partisans who wish to see a distracted country jockeyed into compulsory military service and Protection while it is. distracted, and cannot—as they fancy—see straight and think clearly, that is responsible for this strange conglomeration of ideas and the join- ing together of impossible aims. The coun- try has refused to shut down its businesses, ,and the irealth'of ;England will survive to save Europe as it saved Europe a century ago. The country has resisted the sophistries of the Protectionist, and will continue to do so for reasons as. powerful as those submitted by General Bcinta. It is not the time to talk politics or to discuss tariff schemes, and. we have, on divers occasions, maintained that our trade relations with Germany should be dealt with after the Mins have received their hiding and we know what the actual ecindi- tions are and are likely to be. - But the .Pro. '7' f
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1916. GOSSIP.

tectionists, like their twin brothers the Com- pulsionists, provoke to combat, and Progres- sives must, perforce, be alert lest these wily and persistent champions of re-action strike home secretly. For the moment all, that is necessary is that we should have nothing to do with, either of..these.,hare-braintid schemea except to block them until the mind of the nation is free to deal with them deliberately and rationally.

There is ,one sure line of conduot we can adopt with a view to our future.tvelfare. , We can educate and organise Ourselves if we will s 4;) that the extraneous and artificial aid of Protection will be as superfluous as it is objeelionable. The kind of Protection' that would meet existing circumstances would need to 'try to...,protect home industries and agricul- ture, ''' give .preferential treatment , to our Dominidtis'beyond the seas and India, set ,up , mutually: favourable tariffs among the Entente Powers, erect 'a general -tariff against :neutral nations, and a' particular one itiains present • -enemy countries. The ?clashing of interests here is so pronounced that the tangle is not likely to be straightened out by its ad- vocates .before we have the time and inclina- tion to approach the question froin a national rather than a partisan pint .of view. But there are ná such confounding issues attend- ing the advice to educate and organise. That we are the superior of the Germans in every branch of life, save that of cunning, treachery and the faculty to suck other people's brains, is well established. We, are apt to belaud German Methods and to ape German institu- tions, but in reality we can beat them at any- thing, almost, they care to try. Where they ' beat us is in plodding and combining, while we go light-heartedly into the industrial fray and pull individually for our own ends. At the recent meeting of the 'Royal Society of Arts, Dr. DUGALD CLERK had little difficulty in proving that we outrun Germany in all the leading industries, that we have led in all the great scientific discoveries and inventions, and that th,ct. Germans have followed at a very re- spectful distance, and that our success in colonising and Germany's failure in the same sphere has not been chance or juck. Why, he asked, does Germany, with its order and method, fail, while " unpractical, illogical, idealistic England is successful "1' He answers himself thus :

The ,cause, I believe, is to be found deep down in the nature of the 'respective peoples. The German brain is. deductive, while the English brain is inductive. All German philosophers have invariably been of the deductive type, while among English philosophers only Newton and. Harvey are deductive. Practically all other g are inductive. The deductive brain, allied to stupidity and a curious irrelevance, is characteristically German. and often produces absurd results. Even when legitimately use.l the deductive system is dangerous. It looks far more orderly and brilliant to .deduce a whole :universe from a few general propositions, but in actual life it is much safer and more accurate to rise from the particular to the general rather than descend from the general to the particular. .. . The English have no illu,sien.-about the mightiness of: their intellect. They -do net say, as a German' says, "This should, or must, act in this way "; they ask, "Here are circum- stances, :a hat is- really ,happening?" They observe the circumstances and they -deal with circumstance s largely .as they present them- selves.'" The English always grasp,- however, in war as in peace, the essentials which -must be observed if failure is to be avoided. -The Germans sometimes succeed in their ordered sequence, but 'Nature interferes most rudely and prevents the, accomplishment of things which German 'reason proves to its. own satisfaction should really follow: England grasped the main facts of its existence, protected by water and an industrial population needin; large sup- plies of food from outside; hence, an overwhelm- ing Navy, and behind the "sure shield" of the Navy she knew she would have time' whatever arose, to plan, devise and meet difficulties. In this great war she is doing that, as she ever did. All the appearances called unpractical, illogical or muddling through, is but appearance. Eng- land is not unpractical. She is the most prac- flea' nation in the world.

If it be true that hitherto we have done all the thinking out while the Germans have been living on applying our, discoveries. to practical ends, it would appear that we have a better means to hand for a• complete triumph than the Protectionist nostrum of tariff .barriers such as German " reason !' has devised. ' One of those means is to make a better. use of the Faculty of Commerce at our Universities, as advocated by Mr. F. A. FROST at the last annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce. We must take a bigger share of the results of our pioneer work in the future than we have dono. in the past.

I hear at first hand from one who knows, that Father Lane Fox, whe was wounded at the Front a time back, was one of the most suc- cessful chaplains out there, and was so ex- trem6ly'popular that men of all denominations constantly sought his advice and help. He was always "on the go" from early morning till late at night, often at considerable risk, and with the minimum of rest. '

Last week the first dividends on the ordinary shares of the Manchester Ship Canal were paid. To take a concrete case, I know of the pos- sessor of two .210 shares in Warrington who re- ceived 2s. 7d. That is, in round figures, 30 pence in thirty years on an investment of £2O. A penny a year per £2O is not a big sum; but the fact that the waterway has accomplished what was reckoned to be impossible, and entered upon the -paying stage, is a great .fact.

This week the new rule that only Wounded soldiers are to have the free use of the tramcars and motor 'buses came into operation. The young .able-bodied men who monopolised the conveyances in battalions. crushing out ordinary paying passengers, however old or infirm, have only themselt.es to blanae.now that a very great privilege has been withdrawn from. them.

It is, or course, a thoroughly English custom to abuse a privilege till those granting it repent of doing good. I believe a system of giving passes to the hospitals, to be dealt out to the genuine cases is being perfected. It would be a pity if any wounded were made to suffer, in com- fort or in dignity for the shortcomings of their thoughtless but healthy comrades.

Observation shows that the restriction of freo tramcar rides to soldiers has not greatly aftectei the number who use the ears on the general routes, but the 'buses on the Gorsey-lane route have been less crowded.
Most of the soldiers at the Barracks who were in the habit of riding have taken to walking. A "bob a day" does not allow much for tram rides.

I note with pleaßure that the autht.rities ar not strictly enforcing the regulation that not more than twelve wounded soldiers shall travel free on one journey. Where there is reasonable room for civilians conductors refrain from demanding pennies on the Longford route. This, I know, is much appreciated.

I am told that there is a considerable amount of uneasiness in Rugby football circles locally at the poor quality of the play shown by those who have recently been taking part in the Intermediate League Competition. There is not much promise of the League bringing out talent for the Warrington team Nchen Wilderspool reopens to its regular patrons.

"The Examiner" ventured upon the asser- tion last week, in recording the news of the misfortune which had befallen Major Cros- field at the Front, that there was "not a home in Warrington where the sad news will not be received in sorrow." •

That sentence, experience has proved, was a literally truthful prophecy. When Sir Arthur Crosfield's telegram was received at the works at Bank Quay tears flowed copiously. Others in all parts of the town were affected as they had never before been affected by news from the Front.

Mr. F. J. Coakley, a teacher at St. Mary's Boys'School, who. was called up for active service with the local Territorials on the outbreak of war, has now returned from active service, and has been granted leave of absence from school duty until May Ist.

Miss Dorothy Harding has the honour' of being appointed first "lady srthool attendance officer in Warrington. Her engagement, which is a temporary one, dategfrom March 30th, and will be confirmed at the meeting of the Educa- tion Committee on Monday night.
The site of the proposed Oliver-street Council School is to be placed at, the,die4osal of the Silver-street School for the .pur_pobe-i of a play- ground.

It is evident that the peace foreshadowed by the Chairman of the Education Committee to be arranged between the Health Committee and the Medioal Inspection Committee is about to take effect. Mr. Holman Kingdon has been appointed chairman of the Medical Inspection Committee once again.
An interesting confession—the Archdeacon of Rochdale at the Parish Church yesterday afternoon: "I am no judge of sermons."

div.head: TALKED WITH THE KING.
div.p: TALKED WITH THE KING.
Warrington Engineer's Fortune While In Hospital.

A Warrington soldier has use the honour of a ten rainutes".-chat with King George. The scene of this memorable meeting was at the Royal -Herbert *Vital, Woolwich, which the King visited on,'Saturday. ' It is another typical instance of His Majesty's interest and concern for the welfare of wounded soldiers. The Lance-Corporal, who is in the Royal Engineers, and well-known in the borough and Stockton Heath, where he resides, had been badly wounded in the thigh, and while making a tour of the hospital the King stopped at his bedside and became interested in the details of his wounds. .It was a '.heart-to:-Iieart,..eltat that %followeo The Kingimight have been at the bedsideof one of his own kith and kin, eo concerned was he with the patient's injuries- He • -gat. On the bed, while the nature of the wound and position were sketched and described, br the doctor in attendance. The wound is a remarkable one, the bullet having punched a hole clean through the thigh bone, and the doctor explained to the King that it was the first time in his (the doctor's) ex- perience, he had -known a bullet Pe.netrate the belie in this`fashion, without breaking it com- pletely. Naturally- he is proud of the honour of having chatted with the King, and will ever rerdember the kindly interest IBS plafed, Majesty dis- , Another woun.ded patient, who had the good fortune to possess an autograph album, was honoured. by. the King with his signature therein. These are happy episodes in a scyldier's life; to be remembered and cherished. Before the war the Lancezoeporal was on the engineering staff of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coat , and Iron Co., Ltd., and re• ceived his v,e6und On the 17th Pitiarth. , When crossing the 'channel he had the novel experience of lying in 'bed with a lifebelt t4trapped round him on the hospital ship. ,This precaution, he says, was necessary, owing to the g prevailing short-sightedness of the German sub- marines' commanders mistakin hospital ships for Dreadnclights.

div.head: N AND AROUND A HUT.
div.p: N AND AROUND A HUT.
How "Tommy " Spends His
Leisure With Y.M.C.A.
UNITY AT THE FRONT.
" Tommy " in and around a Y.M.C.A. hut at the Front is a curious and amusing fellow.

A vivid description of his leisure life was offered by the Be. T. T. Jp.mes in the Ladies' Parlour adjoinini.Wycliffe .Church, on Thurs- day, at the conclugiOn of a cafe chantant in aid of the Y.M.C.A. .

_ Here are interesting excerpts from his speech: One of the most amazing things about a British " Tommy "is his appetite. At the base he comes into the Y.M.C.A. hut for something to eat before dinner, then he goes out for the regulation dinner, and tomes back again for something more. He does that regularly. In each hut there is a piano, and it is always being, played—sometimes by those who can play and sometimes by those who think they can. But everyone is allowed to strum the keys, whether he can play or not. Looking after the physical side of men's lives is very important. If a lad could not go into these places for enjoyment it would be very easy for him to go to places ;where there were temptations to intemperance, and where he could lose his moral and spiritual strength. We always look after " Tommy's " social and mental life. We often have concerts in the huts. Sometimes parties come out to us from England and give very good performances. but more often we have concerts on our own. There
is never any difficulty in getting anybody to sing. No soldier is afraid to take Rad in a concert!
We also have leetures regularly. t'roviding man knows what he is talking about. and does not .try to be too eloquent they listen as long as you like.
There are also debating and Shakespeare 'societies.
Where The Front Surpasses Home.

A Y.M.C.A. hut is also a centre Of religious activities, but not in any • .sectarian sense. It is purely unseetarian. It vies indeed my lot to live in an atmosphere of Christian unity such as is very seldom to be found at home. Men of all religious persuasions meet in those huts. . On Sundays we have three church parades. At 10 o'clock, the Presby-

teriansMe; at 11 o'clock, the Nonconformists.; and at 12 o'clock the Anglicans. I do not think these varying times have anything to do with the hour at.which they get up! Then at night we have a service where all of us ministers get mixed up on the platform in extricable confusion, so that it would be im- possible to tell one from the other. I wish we got mixed up a bit more at home in the same way. _ _ -

AU this work refers to that (low at the base. Naturally, when you get nearer to the firin_g_line there is a change, and everything is a good deal rougher and ruder and less well-organised. We have not i.Tot a great many huts near the firing line, for it is not worth while putting them up, because you do not know how long they will stand. Shells are no respecters of buildings. But we are, represented in some places. It is

more usual to -take an old cafe or barn in the village—anywhere where there is,some kind ot shelter. Sometimes we are very near the firing line. Once I asked a fellow how far it was to the trenches, and he said, "Just down the street and turn to the right." I replied. "Thank you very much, but I'm not going at this moment !" Finding's Keeping—As Long As You Can.

In the Army you take what you find and keep it as long as you'can ! I was standing outside my Y.M.C.A. barn one day, when a shell landed in the field just be- hind. "A bit close." I remarked to a soldier. "Yes. That's a Y.M.C.A. shell," he replied. It made a big hole in the garden. It did nothing el—just a bit of gardening for us, , A story went about that an Irish lad wrote home to his mother, "We have had a stormy night in the trenches, being up to our knees in even feet of water."
There' is no snirit of despondency or discour, agoment at the Front. There is noq3ther feeling than that we shall pull through ultimately. If there is any panic or pessimism it exists at home.

The men got fun out of everything imaginable. Once, when the boys were going up to .the firin4 line in London omnibuses one fellow took off his cap and went round for the fares. Some of the patrons asked to be put down .at Bayswater!
Y.M.C.A. work is among the best one can sup- pott

div.head: " SUNRISE " IN DEMAND:

Alderman Bennett's Quotation Of Gladstone's Verses.
