div.head: Air. Gladstone's Verses.
div.p: Air. Gladstone's Verses.

Sir,—lf the paragraph in the "At Random column of to-day's issue concerning Mr. Glad. stone's light verses' intends tok convey the'im presSion• that those quoted were the only one,4 ever published I beg to point out that this is incorrect. Shortly after Mr. (11adstone's death I was shown a copy of a paper called '4 Sun. shine" or." Sunrise," published I believe, in ',Warrington. The,,number in qu,estion contained [an. aecount ,be the great- stateataan's life and the Seenes at Ilawarden at the time of his death, and quoted a poem of several verses written for his favourite grandchild, the then little miss Dorothy Drew, of which I can only recall the following lines:—
I know wheiv there is honey in a jar Fit for a dainty little friend of mine. And, Dorothy, I know where daisies are.
During the years that have intervened since then I, have often felt I would give much to see that paper again and the completion of those lines.
I am, Sir, yours faithfully. ,Jous .fl. RIpREEy. 28,'IZIo6ack-rond, Upper Tooting S:ir.. 131 E.

div.head: Strangling "The Trade."
div.p: Strangling "The Trade."

Alderman John Evans, of Warrington, was elected one of the district representatives on the league council at the annual meeting of the Lancashire land Cheshire District of the Licensed Victualler? Defence League of Eng- land and Wales, at Lancaster, on Wednesday. The report of the Council presented to the meeting alleged that the Control Board Regu- lations had been utilised for strangling "The Triide ".by an insidious process of creeping pro- hibition. "Immune to all' appeal, criticism, or attack from whatever source, the Board has carried out determinedly a preconceived teetotal policy, regardless of necessity, and, being sub- ject to no higher authority than their own whims and fancies, have paid little or no re- gard to appeals for fair treatment. .. . All efforts to convince the Board of non-necessity for this restriction being futile, there was no alternative but to accept the position enforced upon 'us, and naeanwhile, adhering loyalty to the regulations, no opportunity will be lost of get- ting some modification or relaxation of unneces- sAry restrictions."

div.head: Comforts for Soldiers Concert.
div.p: Comforts for Soldiers Concert.

On Saturday, May 6th, in Parr Hall; a grand evening concert will be given, under distin- guished patronage, in aid of the Warrington District of the Voluntary Organisation Scheme ,that has been approved:by the Government for 'profiding comforts fbr' soldiers. The local committee is an amalgamation of the Terri- torial Equipment Fund, the Women's Liberal Association, the District Committee, and the Cairo-street Working Party, and is part of an amalgamation, brought about throughout the country'by the War Office with a view to pre- venting wasteful overlapping. Help •is increasingly needed, and it is, of course, more imperative, than ever that over- lapping should cease and that comforts should be supplied in. a systematic and consequently economical manner. No fewer than 800 Lanca- shire soldiers are known to be prisoners in Germany, so that in this direction the need is great. A really fine programme has been arranged, the artistes including Miss Marie Houghton (soprano), Madame Annie Hargreaves (con- tralto), Miss Mario Xenaky (solo pianist), Mr. Wentworth Minty (tenor), .Captain J. div.head: WHERE VICTORY LIES.
div.p: WHERE VICTORY LIES.
In The Hum Of The Workshop.
CANON SCOTT HOLLAND AT LENTEN SERVICE.
With all his accustomed eloquence and thoughtfulness, the Rev. Scott Holland (Canon of Christ Church, Oxford) delivered a striking
address on "A War in Munitions" at the
Lenten service for men in the Warrington Parish Church last night. There was a large congregation, including men of all denominations.

Taking as his text the words: "Be strong in the Lord," &c., he declared that the war of God was a war of munitions and e4uipment. They had learned the value of those familiar words from bitter experience. They knew now that the secret of victory, the focus of the crisis, and the vital decision did not lie, for instance, in their war in Flanders, not in the shock of charging horses, not in the throbbing trench, not in the agony of the firing line, not in the deadly breach, amidst the bombs and at the end of the bayonet, but far, far back behind in England. They were told that the issue was determined on the banks of the Clyde, the Tyne, the Mersey, and the Deeside, and in Midland and Lancashire towns—in Warrington. It was here at home, out of the sound of the war, without a risk of war—only the roar of the furnace, the hiss of the molten steel, the throb of the hammer, the tap of innumerable tools, the flare of the workshop, the whizzing of wheels, the scream of the saw, the humming boom of drilling holes—all the busy hum of labour. That was where the real work was done; there was the central strain. England relied on the patient, persistent, tireless indus- try of those at home, as well as at the Front. As in the body so in the soul. There was no use concentrating attention merely on the danger spot in this war of God. They had not to limit themselves just to the point of attack. It was not a matter of mere courage and fight- ing forces, or of fire and fury. The winning of the war of God would depend upon their equip- ment and organisation, and for that they would need the preparation that thought an 4 prayer gave them. That would give them the mastery as it gave Pau/ the mastery. Paul was never caught unawares; he always came out on top; he was always the master-man. He was always alert and alive, and the reason for that was that he was "temperate. in all things," which meant that if a man were to excel in life he inuf.t go into training. , The Rev. Canon illustrated his contentions by analogies- in the sporting world, such as running a race or -engaging in a boxing con- test. The competitions were , always won beforehand—in the training ground. If they. in the war of God, did not go into training and discipline themselves they could not expect to win through. To live purely and be above the sins of the flesh they must regulate their will and imagination. In all things they should fight and hold fast. Fight the passion of flesh and the lower man. Disease.in- the flesh was a witness ,of the primi- tive disease in the thought, and the workshop of the brain must be put in order to help the flesh. The struggle of the flesh was a struggle of ignorance against knowledge. It was reason that _gave them the armour to overcome the struggle. The high. spirit of man must come to the rescue of the flesh. 'Unity of mind and bodf should be aimed at, and there should be no 'sealed chamber into which God had not bored. To meet the struggle they needed persistence, not a mere risky start, and when it was all over they wanted a store. of energy, resource anti reserve. It was a continuity of purpose just as in the great battle which was taking place be- fore Verdun. The French were holding back their, reserves, they were in the back ground. The line did not break because the reserve was there; they held back ready to strike with energy, power and resource when the time, came. So it , was with them at home. The armour of Christ would shield them. Whei temptation laid sere upon them they could think of the words "Stand in the armour of God." He called upon them to do their best with the equipment given. div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
Septic Poisoning Causes Renewed Anxiety.
YESTERDAY'S REPORTS.

The latest information respecting Colonel Crosfield is that septic poisoning made its appearance to complicate the wound in his leg, this having been the cause.which necessitated • amputation. • The first news that Colonel Crosfield's wound had taken bad ways came to hand on Tuesday, when a telegram from Sir Arthur Crosfield said that the chief military authority at the hospi- tal in which Colonel Crosfield was lying had wired that the patient had a "badly infected leg, not•yet completely controlled." This suggestion of the presence a septic poisoning of a bad kind was followed by a wire to Bir Arthur Cros- field from his sister; Mrs. Ryan, who had• gone over to France, saying that Colonel Crosfield was going on "fairly well." Mrs. Ryan, writing on Monday evening to Sir Arthur, said:—

"We got to the hospital at six p.m., and the clever London surgeon said that George was going on well, .and that if it were not for this horrid septic poisoning, the ' wound could be closed at once; but of course all the poison must be got out before tilts can he done; )1e said the dressing was therefore painful. . . . He is in a beautiful hospital, with good nurses and a fine surgeon. Mrs. Ryan says she found her brother looking better than she expected. It appears that he had a real set-back on Thursday last week owing to this septic poisoning, and it was then the surgeon wired that the wound was dan- gerous. The pain of the dressings, of course, I takes something ,out of him, but in , between whiles he has not much pain, and with a sleep- ' ing draught every night at 9.30 he gets, a- good ,night's rest. Colonel Crosfield, writing to Sir Arthur a letter dated Monday evening. characteristically refers to anything but himself, excepting in the last paragraph, where he just says: "I shall probably be here for many weeks. It is a slow business battling against the poison." •
HOW THE MISCHIEF WAS DONE.

div.head: REGIMENTAL BALL.
div.p: REGIMENTAL BALL.
South Lancashire Regiment Has Enjoyable Time.
BATTLESHIP AS BANDSTAND.

The members of the South Lancashire Regi- ment, together with their friends, spent a happy time ,on Tuesday evening, when the first regi- mental ball promoted by the battalion was held amid delightful surroundings somewhere in North Lancashire. The fact that the event was in aid of the fund to provide comforts for the Overseas Battalions evoked a ready response to the sale of tickets, and the amount of outside support accorded was .most gratifying. Upwards of 600 were present, and the dancing was generally voted highly en- joyable. The ball was under the patronage of the Com- manding Officer (Lieut.-Col. A. B. Layton) and the officers, many of whom were present. The programme comprised 17 dances, which were eiecutecl to the accompaniment of a choice selec- tion of music by the Regimental Band, ably conducted by Acting-Bandmaster Harper. The platform on which the band was mounted had been cleverly transformed to represent the deck of a battleship, a fact which lent fine effect to .the scene.
Refreshments were served at intervals, and dancing concluded about midnight with the playing of the Regimental March ("God bless the, Prince of Wales") and the National Anthem.

The arrangements were made by the follow- ing committee: Regt.-S.-M. O'Hanlon (chair- man), C.-S.-M. Ryder, C.-S.-M. Dower (hon. sec. and treas.), C.-S.-M. Ridyard, C.-8.-M. Davis, Dronfield, and Sergt. Walker. The following gentlemen also kindly lent assistance: Messrs. A. B. Brown and R. G. Bateson (M.C.'s), C. I. Baker, R. G. Bentley, G. E. Drewery, Geo. W. Bay, It. H. Robinson and C. E. Walton (stewards). - We understand that a creditable sum will be handed over to the comforts fund.

div.head: GLASGOW MALCONTENT.
div.p: GLASGOW MALCONTENT.
Three Years For Ex-School -Teacher.

The trial concluded in the High Court, Edin- burgh. on Wednesday, of John Maclean, ex- teacher, of Glasgow, who was charged under the 'Defence of the Realm Act with making state- , meats at public meetings calculated to prejudice :recruiting and impede munition work. Accused, giving evidence on his own behalf, [denied making use of the words alleved' by the 'prosecution. He declared he never advised ths ' workers to strike, and said the .phrase Down tools" in the indictment occurred in a question put by one of his audience. . The jury, after an absence of sixty-five 'minutes, found unanimously that the prisoner :was guilty on four of the six counts. They held that the charge of advocating a strike at once and the use of guns was not proven. ! In passing sentence of three years' penal servi- tude. his LordshiP said :that prisoner had been found:guilty; not for the first. time, of contra- Cening the regulations for. the !Defence of the Reahh.' div.head: ON HONOUR'S SCROLL.
div.p: ON HONOUR'S SCROLL.
KILLED.
PRIVATE I. SHAW.
Active Socialist And Well Known Billiard Player.

• Unofficial news has reached Councillor James Shaw, 83, Lythgoes-lane, to the effect that his son, Private Isaac Shaw, who belonged to a Welsh regiment, was killed in action on April 3rd. A letter received by Miss Eva Shaw, Private Shaw's sister, from Sergeant C..Furzer, ran:—
I write with 'sorrow these few lines to in- form you that your brother, Ike,' has been killed in action on the 3rd inst. lie was in tny

platoon, and myself and his companions share with you in your bereavement. Your brother was always liked by all of us. I am sorry to say that he was one of about 50 who met their death. But you must cheer up, for he met it bravely for King and -country." Private Shaw, who was 30 years of age and single, was formerly employed as a clerk by the L. and N.-W. Railway Co., at Abergavenny. He left here, however, in August, 1915, and enlisted, after having been refused permission to do so by the company. He was a skilful billiard player, having won several prizes at the Liberal Club. He was an active Socialist, and was a witty speaker. His name appears on the roll of. honour at the Brick-street 'Mission. As a boy he attended Wycliffe School. Another brother, Henry, is serving in the 3/4th South Lancs. Regimental Band.
PRIVATE ISAAC SHAW. Killed in Action.

div.head: Shameless Consciences.
div.p: Shameless Consciences.

As we have said. Isaac. Shaw was a Socialist; hut the call to duty by . his country found him ready. His conscience. was of the typo that led to action in a just cause rather than to inaction in face of threatened disaster. In a letter he wrote so recently as March 29th to his sister, acknowledaing the receipt of a letter, and referring to the loss <if a comrade, he said :---" When I 'look' at .the photograph which I have of his wife and children. I wonder more and more -et the shameless action of the so-called conscientious objectors?, and their miserable pleas for exemption. The majority cannot have a conscience, but many are ci,rtainly objeets."

div.head: PRIVATE R. LEIGH.
div.p: PRIVATE R. LEIGH.
Widow's Two Sons Killed In A Month.
The two sons of. Mrs. Leigh, a widow, 21, Watkin-street, have been killed in the space of a month.

Her eldest son, Lance-Corporal Walter Leigh, was killed in. action op the lath March; whilst on Thursday of this week Mrs. Leigh received unofficial news that her other son, Private Richard Leigh, had been killed. '• A member of the same battalion, writing under date April 11th, said : "I am sorry to tell you that 'Dick,' your son, has been killed. He was guarding a sap in the trenches, -close to the German_ lines, when he received a bullet wound in the head, which caused instant death. He suffered no.
pain. He died a soldier's death for his country."
Captain C. M. Hewlett wrote under • date April 10th:—

-" I wish to tender my heartfelt • sympathies to you in your i•ez:y sad bereavement. I al- way,fi" found your. BO an honest, upright, and trustworthy soldier, and you must feel proud that, as such, he 'gave his life for Sing and country."

Private Leigh, who was 19 years of age, en- listed 'soon after the outbreak of war, having been previously einployed by Messrs. A. Waring and Co., Ltd., tanners, Winwick-road. As a boy he attended St; )3enedictis It.C. School, and 'ivorshipped ;at St.. Benedict's Churcli
lie was granted furlough a fortnight ago, and returned to duty on Wednefiday of last
PRIVATE RICHARD LEIGH. Reported Killed.

div.head: LATE RIFLEMAN JOHNSON
div.p: LATE RIFLEMAN JOHNSON
Killed During Bombardment Of
Trenches.

In our issue. of February 5 we. recorded the death at the Front of Rifleman John Johnson, son of Mr; and Mks.: Wm.-Johnson, 49, Bewsey- rciad, and brother: of • Mrs. McKay, 35, Elaine- street. Full 'news of the manner in which he met his death has um,: reached Mrs. McKay In a letter sent, by a comrade, Corporal J. Cowan. The writer -says " We were holding a line of trenches which were so bad that there,was.scarcely head cover. To mo've ,in the daytime. Meant instant death, and a man wounded during the day could not be removed until darkness set in. On the 21st of January, Jack,, myself and another Corporal were detailed to ',man a bay in these trenches. We were a distanCe of about 50 or 60 yards away from the next-bay, ther.4 having once been the distance of a trenckbetween, but what with the bad weather and tho never ending shelling, it had been beaten down to the level of the ground, making it almost impossible for a man to 'go to the assistance of his comrades in the other bay. The night of the 21st passed with the usual machine-' and rifle fire in all direc- tions, and' I am glad to say that none of our boys were hurt. • . • • • •

div.head: Swept by Artillery.
div.p: Swept by Artillery.

"But on the morning of the 22nd the enemy started with their artillery, sweeping our trenches from left to right. About 10 o'clock in the morning I heard the report of a gun, and all at once felt myself hurled into space, and when I recovered my senses I found that our dug-out had been smashed in. I thought of poor jack and my other mates, and what had become of them. I crawled to where our dug- out was, and found Corporal Shire just recover- ing from the shock. We heard groans proceed- ing from underneath the corrugated iron which had been the roof of our home, and we set to work to uncover the earth. To our surprise we found poor Jack hitd been buried in the debris. As soon as we had got him clear we began to wash the blood from his face and head, and 2is- covered that he was bleeding from a wound in the head. He was unconscious. I and my other mate tried all the first aid methods we knew to try and bring him.round, but all in vain. Poor Jack never regained consciousness.

div.head: Brave Sergeant Assists.
div.p: Brave Sergeant Assists.

"A sergeant named Brimelow, of our platoon, knowing something was wrong, came from his bay, a matter of 200 yards across open ground, to see of what service he could be to us. The enemy saw him and opened fire upon him, but still he kept on until he reached us. We did all we could for Jack, but of no avail. The ser- geant had to retrace his steps, under the same torrent of shot and shell, until he reached his bay: All that day we had to lie on our backs beside your poor brother, not even daring to' get on one's knees. We were bombarded for eight hours, and when darknesgset in we were able to move. We conveyed Jack on .a gtretcher to the ' dressing station, but ,he died without gaining c,onsciousness. The sergeant of whom I have spoken has been mentioned in dispatches, that being his second brave action. Ali Loved Jack.

"We all send our sorrowful and heartfelt sympathy, .for there was no man in th‘ regi- ment more loved and esteemed than Jack. He was always smiling under the worst circum- stances, and many a time 'raised our spirits with his mirth and wit- . It makes us angry to think that such curs as the 'conscientious objectors' should be allowed to remain in Eng- land, when there are men with wives and families helping to crush the Germans out
• Rifleman Johnson was a.Prudential agent and an old boy of the Sacred Heart and St. Alban's Schools. He was also a member of the Junior Liberal Club. •

div.head: RIL 15, 1916.
div.p: THE FIGHT FOR LOOS.
Raddon Court Patient's Vivid Story Of Memorable Day.
GERMAN MACHINE GUNS TURNED ON WOUNDED.

Private J. Tudhope, of the Cameron High- landers, who was seriously wounded: in. the great advance last September,. and is now in Iladdon . Court Military Hospital,„ Latchford; has written to a friend describing in realistic fashion his personal experiences of that historic day. The day before was, spent in receiving explanations of the plan of action, in making final arrangements, and letter-writing. " Our Artillery," he says, " behind us were going strong- and it was line to hear one 'shell follow anOther in. rapid succession without any cessation, The shells went' through the air with a noise like - an, express train with the brakes half on. We could -see them bursting in the German lines.. It was a terrible, yet grand 'sight. In the evening we saw seven aeroplanes directly overhead, scouting. The evening was 'spent in getting rid of all papers, letters, &c., and a long talk among ourselves. Our section all got together, and we fill spoke of the morrow and wondered who would be left when the roll was called, and exchanged farewell Messages. Each wished the 'other good luck, and we lay down on the floor of the trench amidst the bombardment. Of course we did not sleep much. • Things Began To Get Warm.

About four next morning we were -aroused, and the tea dixies were passed up •the' trench. We had hardly begun our breakfast when word was passed down—' Packs, on and prepare to leave the. trench.' Another few Minutes, and the order came down—` Out of the trench . at once,' so breakfast Was left, .and out we got, lined up in the dark, and moved off. Here, then, was the 'beginning of the day- we had been waiting for, and who could tell how many were doing their last march? Yet, withal, everyone was cheerful, and jokes were Old. We passed several of our batteries and entered the communication trench leading to the first line trenches, a couple of miles or so away. We. had . marched, for years it seemed, when the bombardment was renewed with' redoubled 'energy. My goodness, but there was .some noise! We could scarcely .hear ourselves speak. We were half-way when things began to get warm. .We 'heard the' wail of bullets as they went across-the trench; the clap, clap, clap, of the machine guns, and the bursting of shells, not always • our own. Many times We were covered with' earth thrown up by German shells. Suddenly a cry of Shrapnel, keep well down.' We didn't need to be told twice. Even in all this, one of or section, a' chap called -Westwater, was jokink and keeping us in excellent spirits. Then the order No talking' was passed down, so we had a smoke instead. -Westwater asked one chap. for his matches, 'saying, You won't need .them again,' and we all laughed. Ere we had' gone much'' farther, the order came down 'Fix bayonets.' This was done with a few compli- mentary remarks about the Germans. Another order came down, 'smoke helmets' on.'i• Now we -came to a halt near the front trench and waited. The noise was terrific.: How we missed 'getting' a shell amongst us, I don't know. Then a Message Came ‘doWn, 'The, Black Watch has got through.' This was good news, and up our snirits went., On again we went into the first line, and •here were the sealing, ladders for mounting the parapet: Another order 'Was passed down, 'Smoke helmets off, and prepare to charge.' Commercial Traveller As Commander.

"Over we went, lining up as we got over, and before us lay the battlefield. Now each section had its commander, and each platoon - its officer; Our section commander, Sergeant •Douglas Eraser, ,-who was .a traveller in the woollen trade, and who Used to visit Bueeleuch Mills, a.splendid chap, kept us in hand. -Ease off to the left, No. .14; don't bunch,' was the order, and on we swept. Everything was shrouded in blue-grey Smoke, and the field looked awesome. The first German trench was liretty .well batte-rea;•, Una; their barbed . wire y:as well .demolished.. I had. just' cleared The first trench. when someone shouted, Hallo, Jock.' I turned • round, and here was my old hum, Joe Borthwick, lying with some other Gor.. dons, waiting their turn, and he was smiling as if he was enjoying it. I only had time to shout, Hallo, Joe,' and had to move, on. It put new heart into , me, seeing a Langholm face. Poor Joe! I have since heard he was reported missing and now killed. He was a fine chap, and one of the best pals one could wish for, always smiling. Wounded in the Hour of Victory.

"TO return to the fight, we kept going strong, and there was no time to feel afraid. Somehow I felt an Overpowering desire to do or die,;and,l wondered' howlong .1 would keep going without getting knocked out. All round me 'were the greaning of the wounded and the still forms of the dead. I was going strong, and we had cleared .about five trenches of one kind and another, and Loos lay just in front, when suddenly I felt a rip in the arm and a hit in the back; like the kick of a horse-- result, down I Went, , hit by . shrapnel. It would be about eight in the morning when I was Wounded.. I lay just in front of Loos Towers, familiarly known as the Tower Bridge. . "I need not enter into details regarding the issue of the attack, as you will have read many' .times how the Highlanders fought and cleared everything before them. . "I remained conscious when I was hit, and expected to -get another every minute, for I was directly in the fire zone. There floated into ray mind the lines -Which my chum, Jim Moyes, often used' to quote, beginning: , Oh for a lodge in some vast wilderness.'

"After a while 'the firing died down, and our chaps were busy routing the Germans out of Loos, and'l km several batches of prisoners marched back by' CameronS. I began to get stiff and couldn't move, so I had to lie on my stomach. Our chaplain came round and took off my equipment, gave me a drink of water, and,'best of all, a cigarette. .Fancy smoking a cigarette! About one o'clock the Otretther- bearers came round and dressed me, and I told them it was my back, and that I had lain as still as possible, as I didn't know how much I was injured. They cut my tunic, kilt and shirt; and 'wheri"they saw it they said I had oared ray life by doing 'so. This was humorous, wasn't it? I ,thought so,' anyway, and the bullets and shells buzzing about. They then said the stretchers would be round shortly. However, the' Germans had spotted I wasn't dead, so whenever anyone came near me, they turned a machine gun on me from the Towers, another instance of ' German Kultur.' I must have lost myself, for when I came round again it was getting dark, and I was -wet through. Now the reinforcements' began to line Up, and our artillery also, and the horges fairly gal- loped. They were a good way from me, but I don't think, any were hit. What Whizz-Bangs Are Like.

"The Germans then, began to send 'over whizz-bangs. You can hear them coining, and, to give you 'a little idea of what they are like, I ask yo).1 to think of the, back string of a violin being smartly pulled. That is one corn- ing. It bursts, and you hear a noise like a shower-bath wider high pressure, then the contents fall. They began to fall very near me, and it seemed as if my end was going to be violent One burst just in front of me and covered me with•earth, se I began to try and move. After six attempts I got on to roy hands and knees, but I couldn't get up. Then I would crawl 'rather. than lie down again. I tiovr smile when I think of my , appearan* Aly Balmoral cap was sitting on the top of my head like a wet sponge, my, tunic was in rib- bons at the back, my kilt was hanging on to me, as the stretcher-bearers pinned it anyway. Oh! that crawl; every .tithe a star shell went up (the Germans have very fine star shells, which are fired from a pistol, these burst and show a bright light, which light up the cOun- try for miles) down I had to get till the light died "away, and then it took me 'about ' ten minutes to get up again: I was enjoying my- self finmensely. I Crawled fully a mile in this fashion and Came tcii a-German trench between me and a road. Oh; the smell of that trench! I got'on to my' feet-tat least 'I think .I.did— shut. my eyes and jumped. I landed on the far side, and crawled to tbe.road, where' I lay down. among .borges and 'men who had been
Centlowed Rut tolunin.

div.head: PANEL DOCTORS' CHARGES.
div.p: PANEL DOCTORS' CHARGES.
Insurance Committee And Private Fees.
A MISTAKE RECTIFIED.

subject of considerable importance to in- sured persons was dealt with at a meeting of the Warrington Insurance Committee, on. Thurs day night, arising out of a report presented by the Medical Service Sub-conimittee. It aPpeared. .that the sub-committee had received a com- munication from an insured person through her father regarding a panel doctor who had tient in* two accounts amounting to .23 6s. to the father of the insured Person, for *profeSsionar attendance. The insured person had been on the doctor's list from January, 1913, till February,.l9l6, when a." consent to transfer" form, duly signed by the insured, person, and •two.doctors, was received by the committee, and the transfer was efftcted. `rho amount charged was in reference to professional treatment in. July and October of last year. From state- ' =wits made by the doctor and .the father, the latter asked the practitioner to treat him and his daughter about October, 1914; as private patients, as he !` was not satisfied with panel treatment." As this request was persisted in, the practitioner consented. The man was under the impression that the doctor had forthwith taken steps to remove his name, as well as that of his daughter, from the panel list, but he had recently discovered that this was not done. His grievance was not so much against paying the doctor's private account as against the doctor receiving payment from the Insurance Com- mittee also.

The doctor stated. he was under the impres- sion that the names were removed from his list, and if he had broken the regulations he had done ,so quite inadvertently. . The finding of the sub-committee waskthat the doctor, in charging, and receiving 6s. for treatment, which the insured person was en- titled to free of: charge, he had inadvertently contravened clause 2 (ii) of the agreement entered into, with the Insurance Committee, namely, "the practitioner shall not accept any fee or other remuneration in respect of treat- ment which he is required to give." Mr. W. E. Rigby, who had conducted the in.. sured person's claim at the inquiry, said he would aecept the recommendation if they would add a rider that insured persons were acquainted with their position under . their contract with the doctor, and that circulars be printed con- taining extracts of the particular clause for dis- tribution, as far as practicable, among insured persons. He was Sorry to say that this case was not a solitary one. It was one of those rare cases in which they had a person who was public-spirited enough to come forward and. put himself in, perhaps, the odious position of fight- ing his own medical practitioner.

div.head: PROTEST AGAINST INSINUATION.
div.p: PROTEST AGAINST INSINUATION.

Mr. Bibby expressed disagreement with Mr. Rigby's suggestion that they should go to the expense of issuing circulars. He thought the medical faculty were not at all to blame. It was a well-known fact that there were people who were willing to use any means whatever to get what they considered a little extra treat- ment. In this case the man thought he would influence the doctor by offering to become a private patient. He strongly. Protested against the insinuation that the doctor tried .to get at the back of tho Act.
Mr. T. Magsey considered that it was the duty of approved societies to inform their members of their c,ontraets with doctors and their mean- ing. -- _ _ _

The Chairman (Mr. P. Delaney) remarked that it would cost oefpl to have circulars printed and distributed. An insured person, be said, was entitled to the very best possible skill a doctor was able to give. Other members thought publicity in the Press would be quite ample. Mr. Rigby moved that circulars be printed and distributed, as far as practicable, among in- sured persons in the borough in order to let them know their position under their contracts with the doctor.
Mr. W. J. Rowland hoped the committee would not start sending out slippings of the Act. He thought the societiee should pass on the in- formation.

Mr. Dicken said at the meeting the doctors agreed that a mistake had been made, and de- cided to rectify it in the best possible way. The committee had also agreed to accept amends for the mistake. It was a case of two blacks would not make a white. He thought they should adopt tho report in its entirety and let the matter drop. Mr. Rigby's motion was put to the meeting and defeated.

div.head: FIGHT FOR LOOS.—Continued.
div.p: THE FIGHT FOR LOOS.—Continued.

killed by a shell. I envied them being out of pain. I lay hero about an hour, and an officer coming along gave me a drink of water, and said he would send a stretcher for me. Nameless But Glorious Graves.
Royal Court.

"I was then carried for a mile, and as it was nioonlight I saw xnany, many soldiers lying peacefully at 'rest,- be.yond earthly cares. How many of our Scottish chums nOwt lie under a foreign soil in a nameless grave? No more will they see their loved ones, no more will they see the hills of Auld Scotland. They cannot hear, the wind sighing over the hills, and they cannot hear the ripple of the burn as it goes on its course, but who can say they are not better' than us? They fought for the freedom of our country, and they have .passed beyond the veil, and one can almost hear the glorious strain: 'And glory, glory dwelleth in Emmanuel!s land.' • "After being carried a mile I was 'laid down on a waterproof sheet. This was at cross-reeds. By now the moon had risen and everything was clearly seen. On my left lay a French town held by Germans. Further still to the left were two large fires, supposed to be Ger- man magazines. Loos lay behind one. The roads were blocked with infantry ammunition wagons, gun limbers, transports, field kitchens, and dear only knows what, all moving up to the line. I was within an ace of being run over, but 'luckily the driver saw. me. I lay 'hero for throt, hours; and, oh, it was eold ! I was beginning to lose myself again, when a 'chap .ronied me and told me" the road was blocked and the ambulances couldn't get down. He lifted me 'on to my feet and half carried me one and a half miles to the dressing station. The road, was all torn up, huge shell holes being quite COMMOtI, and everything in mud a foot' deep. Wagons were stuck, and the road was one long line orvehicles. Only A Typical Cate. '

"At last I reached the dressing station, where I fainted beantifully twice; and really it was worth it, to get away from the work!. . for even a few minutes. Do not think I am boasting any in relating my experiences. God forbid My Cis° is....typical of runny; :aye and there were hundreds worse, was; lucky in some ways.
.`;‘Froin th 4 dreesing'•etation, to my arrival at this haven of reet is anothor siory, •which I can give •you Uteri:Go with the hope I hare not wearied you, I lay aside the refl."
STAGE AND KINEMA.
I should like to congratulate Mr, Harry Warburton en having been appointed Manager at the Royal Court Theatre. He has been acting-manager lor eight years, but has always looked like a manager.
He has the theatrical appearance and tem- perament in a marked and pleasant degree, romanticism and business capacity 'blending admirably. Urbane in Manner, his popularity is unmistakably high.

Mr. Warburton is a gentleman of ideas and ideals for the theatre, and I think we shall note some .progress at the Royal Court this summer. For One thing, he intends having the place re- decorated, although in the ordinary way of events this is not yet due.

The new manager takes over the " bookings " at the end of June. What plays lie has in store for us I have more than the faintest idea, but, of these, e;letails a few weeks hence. They in- clude some West End successes. I hope they will be successful here. too.

Blackpool is noted for its sea, promenade, and, I have heard, enormous holiday crowds. " Heare-o !" the revue being staged this week may be added to the list. It was created in Blackpool, groWing out of a little alfresto show into the proportions we have seen this week.
It has some capital artistes, and catching ideas, and all it requires to sustain its popti- lariiy is to grow a little more. Its presentation does not last long enough.

As Bill Stickers, Charley Harvey has proved a cheery, old salt, full of good humour. The youngster who played the Middy was his son. He .intends following in the footsteps of his dear, not old, dad. Mr. Harvey has two sons at the Front, one of whom has been wounded. I hope their shots get home as frequently as their father's jokes—always.

Mr. Tom Howell, who takes the part of Ginger, the Bo'sun, has displayed rare vocal • talent. lie has toured in grand opera, having been with Denhof when he made a success of Wagner's " I asked him why be did not stick to grand opera, and he replied, "There is more money in this."

Mr. Hal Bryan, the pleasant Captain, used to be a single turn, but prefers revue because "It is very nice to have a crowd round you." For that you have either to become a Strand police- man or go into revue. Ho chose the latter, and is eminently successful.

Miss Rene Ash, the daring and charming . . leading lady, has been at the Palace and Hippo- . drome in "Violet and Pink." She was with that successful show for about eighteen months. and then wanted a change. "Being in the same . revue and doing the same thing night after night twice over is tiring," she confessed to me.

, Her most taking song this week has been "Come and cuddle me." Her manner of sing- ing it is to make a direct appeal to the young , li , ' 11 men sitting in the stalls to skip over the 11 • orchestra into her arms. 1

Not a few times has this occurred in .some of the' towns she has visited. Only last week at Northampton, Sergeant Healy, the ex-champion boxer, ventured on the stage and gave her a kiss. I expect he shook hands on it—as becomes a boxer.

Another play founded on the Rosary is to be staged at the Royal Court Theatre next week. Beauty of presentatiou is to be its marked feature. It is entitled "His Mother's Rosary," and has a war flavour.

Hippodrome. • • Mr. Devant, the illusionist, was enthusiastic- ally heralded and ho has come ,up to paper form. Large houses have observed him and compared his tricks and methods with those of • Chung Ling •Soo, Linga Sing, Morritt, and others. It is not simply with the mystery and elaboratonevg of_ his tricks that Mr. Devant scores: his charm and apparent non-chalance are unsurpassed.

I say "apparent non-chalance" for the reason that just now ldr. Devant is not par- tiaularly well and, naturally, in a business like his, where speed and subtlety predominate, he is not working without anxiety. However, things have gone smoothly, and the new illusions he has introduced have been mystify- ing in the extreme..

'The most interesting pictures on our noardings during the last ten days have been those adver- tising Devant and all his works. They are a new selecticn this year, and gre the work of that perfect artiste John Hassan.

•Devant believes,whole-heartedlY in advertising largely. In some cities he spends more than Or, a week in this. way. " Providing you have a good show and don't disappoint your public, advertising pays for the trouble and thought entailed," he remarked to me. Or, as the com- mercial department says, " ' Ads' add to your profits."

There is to be something extra at the Palace and Hippodrome next week. Apart from the usual performances in the evening, at which variety artistes will appear, there are to be matinees each afternoon for one purpose—the exhibiting of the great film, "Britain Pre- pared." It has the blessing of the Admiralty, War Office, and Ministry of Munitions. When screened for the ,first time—not long ago—Mr. Balfour was a ,spectator, and afterwgrds made a speech, in which he used the word "Won- derful."

When we see it I believe we shall say the same. It depicts the New Army in the making-- Infantry, Artillery, Cavalry and Flying Corps —and shows them in training for the fray on the other side of the Channel. 100,000 men and women are also seen making ammunition.

Afterwards there is "The Sure Shield of e. Britain and Empire"—to wit, the Navy. , Herein we have the building and launching of a battleship and everything associated with the Navy. We shall be able to observe that acme , of the seas we have all heard about—the Grand Fleet—as well as life on the Queen Elizabeth.
. The Mayor and Mayoress (Alderznan and Mrs. Peacock), Colonel' Moggridge and Captain Mathain§ have promised their patronage: • ;

Of course there will..be the usual vaudeville entertainment in the evenings. The Keystone Comedy Cyclist& head the bill, and May Sherra.rd is another first-rater. She is called the "new style comedienne," and her merits in the music-hall world may be judged from the fact that she is booked up until 1920.

The kinemas. i" When We Were Twenty-one" proved a great attraction at the "Star" in the beginning of the week. "The Angels of Mons" and the "House of the Lost Court" are the two principal films now showing.

For next s week we are promised a galaxy of good things in the form of a different star Pic- ture each day. They are all from the studios of the famous Players Co: and the Lasky Co.. so wp may• anticipate a first-class entertainment. There will be two performances on Good Friday, at six and eight.
Among .the tittractionS coming. shortly will be .filin version of the 'famons novel, ". The DO Doctor," by "'David. Deban," the .eininent authoress.

Fine programmes% hat,e been presented this week at the Picture. HonSecin Wfiimrteigh- street. "The Shabbies "—a splendid picture— topped the bill during the first half of the week, and "'Alice of Hudson Bay" during the last half.'
ur- ing tho first half of next week "Tile

div.head: tttas to the Oita
div.p: tttas to the Oita
THE CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR.

Sir,—Though as I stated in-my last letter, I do not intend to pursue the controversy regard- ing the conscientious objector, Councillor Roberts's letter, which appeared last week, and is hich concerns me personally, demands a reply. A commentary on the reason I gave for not coiltinuing the controversy is reported from South Wales. A miner, named Smith,: at Abertillery, wrote. a letter 4,etending -conscien- tious objectors and took it to the editor of a local. paper. The result was that instead of the letter appearing, Smith was arrested by the police, and is now awaiting trial. TO distort the reason I gave into confession of a want of pluck and a desire to save my own skin, sounds strange from Councillor Roberts. For a person with the " powers .that be " and, the popular cry on his side to attack a Smal4 unpopular minority, bound hand and foot and not permitted to state their case, does not re- quire great courage. But for such a person to make his attack anonymously surely reveals cowardice and a lack of manliness if not some- thing worse. Sly opinion of any one who can bring himself to adopt such a method remains as I have stated, in spite of all 'Councillor Roberts's hysterical raving. However, having "drawn the badger," I rest content, and do not intend to write again, what- ever Councillor •Roberts may reply.—Yours. tke , H. T. DIXON. ".Ilighfields," Penketh, AV:trriagton.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS AND lIESTRIC-
div.p: DRUNKENNESS AND lIESTRIC-
TIONS.

Sir,—lt is no use YOUr co'rrevondcut,' Mr. Simpson, suggesting that the police authorities deliberately slacken Or whip up their energies to snit the convenience of, the Control Board. I for one, and 'I am sure there are many others who will not, do not accept such a suggestion; and the comparisons used in the correspondence between us were not based upon the period Of the "four preceding weeks," as he says. If he will refer to "The Examiner" of February, 26th he will find that I used a five months' com- parison, i.e., not four, but twenty .Weeks, namely August to December in 1914 and 1915, which, in Liverpool, showed a decrease under restriction of 44 per cent. of drunkenness record. He is unable to .substantiate' his attack upon what he is pleased to call the "Teetotal theory," and so charging the-Paige authorities with even assisting that theoit7 byestating io,his last letter that "in London and LiverpOolAhe arrests for the four weeks preceding the introduction of the regulations showed a very suspicious leap up- wards." Evidently Mr. Simpson has a bad case, but he does not iraprov,e it by throiving suspicion upon our administration. Our case is verified not only by police records, but also by the records of our factories and workshops: Less beer, better time; more re- strictions, greater efficiency and larger output even of munitions.' The Control Board must go forth and, assisted by the restricted manufac- ture as Well as hours of sate, much good will be accomplished.and, we shall be helped to realise the great 'benefits-that would accrue if we as a nation would not allow onrsetves to -be, domin- ated by the influence of the Trade. These re- strictions are only part of the larger question, Drink or victory? The Czar of Russia answered " Victory " •. France answered "Victory"; and what shall we answer? At • any rate, the teetotaler says "Victory," and I am on their side. BENJ. T. PARKES..

div.head: £lOO,OOO Damage Done At Highfield's, Runcorn.
div.p: £lOO,OOO Damage Done At Highfield's, Runcorn.
GIRLS HELP FIRE BRIGADES.

. . Tho Warrington Fire Brigaile, along with several other brigades, was engaged many hours on,Friday :night and Saturday morning fighting a disastrous fire which broke out at the High- field Tannery, Runcorn. The damage is esti- mated at. £100,006, and is largely covered by in- surance.

The offices, warehouse; stores and part of the works were gutted, and- large .quantities of finished leather and leather being -put .through , . the tanning'proceSSeS; perished in the flauiesi;lt is supposed that the fire started it the top of the hoist in the centre of the works. . It was about six o'clock on Friday night when one of the "workinen discovered smoke issuing from the .sheds, and very soon flames burst forth. The works' fire engine was brought out and played on the*.fl-re, to he soon folrowed by the Runcorn. Council Brigade. The danger of the flames spreading to other buildings was realised, and hundreds of willing helpers, in- cluding many girls, _worked with energy in re- moving valuable business books and papers, also furnitureirom Ike -office, while workmen busied -themselves in 'removing a considerable quantity of finished leather from the warehouse and barging it across the canal;

div.head: SEEN FOR MILES AROUND.
div.p: SEEN FOR MILES AROUND.

, Spreading rapidly, the whole of the main part .of - the tannery—about two hundred yards in 'length and the same in depth—be- came enveloped in flames. As the darkness approached, the sight was one of regrettable splendour, the glare of the flames lighting up the surrounding district, and the fire could be seen from any point of vantage for many miles around. The roof of the structure collapsed, and the flames were followed by dense clouds of smoke, many teaks of oil- being attacked by• the fire. • -

The walls of the structure were cracked, and telephone wires on the poles opposite the worlis,, broke and fell on one of the fire engines. Two hundred gallons of oil stored in the tanks WPM destroyed, in addition to the ruin brought upon the offices and warehouse. Fortunately, the Hine yard and chrome yard were left intact,- together with praotically all of the valuable mOttincry. Na employes will, be thrown out of Work:, as they will be trans- ferred to the Camden works in High-street, and the labour of others will-be utilised at the Pen- keth Tannery, wherelhe salvage will.be finished. Three firemen were injured, hut happily not seriously. One fell in the canal, but was quickly rescued.

div.head: CALL TO THE WARRINGTON BRIGADE.
div.p: THE CALL TO THE WARRINGTON BRIGADE.

It was a few minutes after seven on Friday night that an urgent request for help was re- ceived at the Warrington Fire Station by Supt. Turner, who at once disliatched the motor fire engine in charge of 'Deputy Superintendent Cook and Engineer Wakefield. When the Warring- ton contingent arrived, after a rapid run, the roof of the affected part had fallen in, and the fire was spreading towards the north portion of the works. Efforts were directed to the saving of the lower part of the works, valuable assist- ance being given by employes. The brigade had -700 yards of hose in use, and. two hours' hard work resulted in cutting off the fire from the sheds threatened. -The- brigade remained on duty all night, playing upon the smouldering debris. When the ruins had cooled down the engine was withdrawn, and arrived home aboht ten o'clock on Saturday morning.

div.head: AN OLD-TIME – COMPARISON.
div.p: AN OLD-TIME - COMPARISON.

Deputy-Superintendent Cook, interviewed by "The Examiner" representative, said he thought the coinbined efforts of the four bri- gades had succeeded in effecting a very good stop, as most .of tho buildings were made of wood. "We got a fine round.6l cheering from the crowd on our arrival,' he said. " We,were given ,every assistance by the managers, Mr. P,osnettand Mr. Johnson'. I was asked to direct the operations of the combined brigades, placing the firemen where they could best work with advantage. About 12 jets were directed across this part of the premises. Most of tile firemen worked well under -trying conditions, especially later in the evening, when the footing on the frost-bound bent roofs was very treacherous, and falls were plentiful." ..•

Mr.. Cook recalled the last time the works were burned down, 23 years ago to-day on a Friday. lie remarked that he got there much quicker this time. On that occasion he and three other' firamen had ,to goon foot, a task firemen would not relish in these days. There were two manual engines there then. Our present Super- intendent was also there, the damage being .225,000.

div.head: FINE "TEST."
div.p: A FINE "TEST."

Both the Runcorn .Fire Brigade and the High- fiebi Tannery Brigade got steam fire engines less than -a month ago. .They had a fine test to start with. The Warringqin. Fire Brigade's motor engine's powerful streanis were very effec- tive, and worked well for about .13 hours. Mr. Posnett and Mr. Johnson were on the scene all night and worked untiringly. Some difficulty was experienced in getting .through meSikigeto for -assistance owing to the telephone wires being burnt down very quickly. This accounts for the Warrington Brigade hay- in t a late call. They, however, last no time when they started.

Sapper Percy Clare.—Writing to his Mother at . Booth's Hill, Sapper Percy Clare states:—"l "am pleased .to say that we are all first rate ' out here. „We came down from the trenches to-day, but ffave to go up again to- night for another day; but keep on smiling, we shall pull through, and we arc far from being downhearted yet. Remember we are winning, and with a little hick. We shill.be,with.you be- fore long." Prior to joining the Royal Engineers. Sapper Perry Clare was a local Territorial.

British and Foreign Bib-le Society.—The annual: public meeting of the Lymm branch of the -above society was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom on Monday evening, when an interesting lantern lecture as given by the Rev. T. A. Wolfendale, entitled "The Bible in South Africa and iii the trenches of Europe." There was a good assembly. The chair • was taken by Mrs. T. J. Ridgway, who, in a few well- choen words, pleaded the society's cause. Mr. W. T. Moss 'officiated at the lantern. At the close of the. lecture a collection was :made on behalf of the funds of the society..

Sergeant J. H. Moston in Hospital.—Writing from Maten Hospital, Belfast, to Mrs. Geo., Davies, of Booth's Hill, Sergeant J. H. .Moston states :----" I have not been so very well lately, so have, had to stop indoors, suffering from pains in the hack of My head; but this being a nice day, the .doctor -says I might go out this afternoon. This is a beautiful place,' and .very convenient, for the moment you get through the hospital door, you can get on -a•ce,r,and be up,in the country in a very short time.'!, 'Sergeant J. Moston was sent to hOspital from the Front a short time age, suffering from a nervous break- down.

Death of an Ex-Volunteer.—We regret to an- nounce the death of ex-Sergt. William Kirk- patrick, which took place at his residence, the Bridgewater Arms, early yesterday morning. He was a member of the old 3rd Vol. Batt. Cheshire Regiment (now Territorials) for a period of over thirty years, and retired under the age limit. Up to a short time ago he held the position of captain to the local fire brigade, but was compelled to resign owing to ill-health. .His three sons are now with the colours, two of them being on active service. The interment will take -place on Monday afternoon at LTinm Parish Church.' '

Lymm Soldier Killed in Action.—News has just ' been received to the effect that Private James White, of the Scots Guards, formerly a Lymm man, has been killed inaction during a bombardment. The news was, received through the medium of a letter sent by a comrade to his sister, Miss Maggie White, of Mere, and after- wards to his brother, Mr. Robert White, cabinet maker, of the village. White was a well-known Lymm man, and served his apprenticeship as a draper to Mr. R. H. Gotobed, afterwards going in business as a draper at Southampton. He was 35 years of age, and was educated at Lymm and Oughtrington. Schools. He worshipped at Oughtrington Parish Church. Further par- ticulars are not yet to hand.

"Reminds One of Home."—Writing to his mother at West Hyde, Newfields, from some- where in the war %one, Corporal Henry Brookes states: .`titt the time of writing the weather is glorious and the surroundings at. this place remind one much of home. The song of the bells which leaps from the small church tower away in the distance seems to cheer one after a march from the trenches. So different are the sounds Up there! This week we have been very fortunate in meeting a few more of the men from our village. It is nice to see the old faces and to spend a quiet hour with them." Corporal H. Brookes, it will be re- membered, holds 'the Order of St. George (2nd Class) for distinguished ambulance work while under fire.

£7OO For Mouth Organs.—An organ recital was given at the Parish Church on Sunday evening, when Mr. Win. Cooke, organist and choir- master, delighted a fairly large gathering with :several selections. including " Pondino 1" and "Concerto," by W. Sherndale Bennett, and 4archl' ("Calvary") by Richard Wagner: This recital was the last of a series of three, which have been given for the purpose of raising money to provide mouth organs for our soldiers and sailors. The "Musical News " urged all organists throughout the country to give recitals in order to raise a fund to provide these instru- ments. "So with the kind consent of the church- wardens," says Mr. Cooke, "I arranged for three recitals to be given, one each month, and for a plate to be .held at the -door to .catch the contributions of the benevolent as they passed out; and by these means I have been able to collect the sum of £5 15s. lod. The national fund is now close on £700." At the commence- ment of the war the choir boys gave fourteen mouth organs to the fund.

Funeral of Mrs. Newton, of Warburton.—lt is with regret that we announce the death and funeral of Mrs. Newton, of Birch Farm, War- burton, at the age of .56 years. It is only two years since the death of,,Mr.:Newton„ and much sympathy will be felt ,for the four sons and four daughters who are bit. The funeral took place at Rostherne, the Bev. Jeffery J War- birton officiating.

Blue Cross Fund.—With .the ALeil Cross ,fund, and all the other numerous charities going full swing, some kind-hearted residents are giving a little thought to the poor horses that are con- stantly getting maimed in the various theatres of war. A concert is to be held an the 26th in the Congregational Schoolroom, its object being to raise money to help the sufferings of our wounded horses. ,

, Death Of Old Resident.—The death took place at his residence, Cherry-lane, on Sunday morn- ing, of Mr. David Vast, a-_ytreil-known resident, at the age of 67, after a brief illne. He was very =inch respected in the district, and followed the occupation of a gardener. . The in- terment took place at the Parish Church on Wednesday afternoiifi, and was witnessed by r-: large circle of relatives and friends. The large number of floral tributes received marked the deep 'respect in which he was held in the district.

Captain G. W. C. Hartley. Home Fram The Front.—Amongst the latest arrivals from the Front is Captain G. W. C. Hartley, who certainly looks the picture of health. Captain Hartley, at the time of mobilisation, held the rank of Second-Lieutenant, but his ability was son recognised; and he was promoted to the 2rdtk•4sf Captain:. and befare, 16ng was bne of the, most popular officers in his battalion. Numerous letters sent by the local "Terriers "'testify the good will and deep respect they hold for their gallant Captain.

He also stated that when he was attested he was only passed for home service. His wife was a semi-invalid.

div.head: TRIBUNAL APPEALS.
div.p: TRIBUNAL APPEALS.
tVar Worker Dying To Get into The Army.

At the Lymm Military Tribunal eleven claims for total exemption were made-for eleven work- men for. a firm engaged on GovernmJut work. An adjOirriment Of" the 'easel was asked for because, it was. understood that the men' would shortly be placed on the list of reserved trades and would be granted badges and certificates. The representative of the firm, when asked whether one of the men was single and only 21 years of age, replied: "The man referred to is simply dying to get into the 'Army, and only approached ma on the subject last week, so 1 have decided to let him go providing you give me a week or two to replace him." This man was granted temporary exemption until the 30th of April. The remaining cases were. adjourned until May sth.
Temporary Exemption.
A infiffiea man ,appllecl for total exemption for business reasons. Ile stated that he was

, . Writing. to. his.,,rnotlier. at.Moston-street, New- fields,- Private James lennings, Of the Manches- ter 'Regiment,- states : " You will notice by the address that I am back in the old company, as they have put all the Maxim gun sections together, and posted us all to one company. I have received a letter from Wm. Taylor, of the Army Cycle Corps, in reply to the one I sent him, and we are both: surprised to learn that we are not above three miles aprt, and perhaps not 300 Yards, for all we know. I was surprised when I saw his ad- dress; he is in exactly the same place as me; it is a plane called , so by the time you re- ceive this letter I hope we shall have met. I am sorry to heaf7 that my brother Sam is in hospital suffering With his teeth. I suppose he will be having them out. People say that there Is nothing like your awn, but I wish I had had mine .out for they have given 'me a lot of trouble lately. He says that he does not like this place. Well I don't suppose he.-does, fqr it is very hot.. But taking the place on ,a whole, it is a beautiful country. You say •by your letter that they are making all the single men of military age join the colours. Well, it is about time something was done to bring the slack?rs up, for it is only fair to us that are trying to do our bit to defend the old country. Why should we that are out here suffer the trials, of War, while others are allowed to go scot free and live in luxury at home? They don't seem to realise what it would mean it the Germans hap- pened to get into England and violate it, the same ,as they -did to littlellelgiuM.- and France. I. see by the papers that -Lyinni, like all' other towns, is guarding againAt, 'posSible raid‘s by .hostile.aircraft. .It Will. make it very awkward getting, about at ,night, .but -there are all sorts. -of inconveniences in war time, and you will have to put up with them." - 'Private James Jennings is u well-known local -lad, .and priorto the war wi 'employed at Irlam. The brother, Sam, to whom he refers, is the one who was killed in action a short time ago.

Mrs. ,Brindley was born at Runcorn, in. 18.58, and.came: to Warrington about ;33 years ago. Alter many years spent. in business as a milliner in Butter Market-street, Mr. and Mrs. 'Brindley retired„ .and have spent the last 14 years at their: home in • Whitefield-road. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Adult School Activities.—The past month has been fuller than usual of activity in this school. Following the successful reading of f`Julius:.Cfe,sar" by.members; the first bulb show has s been held, Alija also Proved to be most encouraging; and indicated the great possibili- ties for .future usefulnesS which lie in this direction. There were about fifty entries, con- taining seventy separite exhibits. Although _many of the rqembers .were taking up this•fas-- cipating hebby .fcii" the first time, the results' were Sucli..as to make them resolve to study and- practise further in this direction. There were fine specimens of hyacinths, tulips and daffodils on the stands. A very popular competition was that for a decorative vase or bowl. of cut *flowers. Credit is due to the Show Committee for the admirable wain. which it was carrie:l out. This new departure, which may be traced to the. seed-sowing .done by the Stockton Heath Garden ,Society, will doubtless no be a per-. inanent branch of the work/of the school. • • The next event :was h. very •successful whist drive kot up .by members on ,behalf of neees- series for-the prisoners.of.war.in Germany. The. prizes and refreshments were provided . various members; the whole of the., proceeds being given in equal shares to the. 'Lancashire and Cheshire funds. A sum of RA 68. was realised. The other activities of the school are in a healthy state, the leeturettes on Sunday morning being highly appreciated and profit- ably discussed by the members., , The women's school is in an equally prosperous condition.

div.head: BURTON WOOD.
div.p: BURTON WOOD.

Farmer's Sudden Death.—While working, in a field, Mr: James Briers, of Brookside Farm, Burtonwood, was observed to fall.. These en- gaged near him, run to ,his assistance, but it was found that he was dead. Mr. Briers, who was for many years a corn .merehant in Liver- pool, was well known on the local corn markets and was highly respected for his genial manner and quiet humour. Much sympathy ig ex- pressed for his widow and family.
Mixed Company. Sentry (at Remount Camp) : "nalt; who goes there?" • Weary Vn:ce "One friend and to —"Punch."

The correspondence included the receipt 'of d letter from the Warrington Coroner, calling the Council's attention to what he described as a scandal, of a body being found in the canal at Sankey on a recent Sunday afternoon, and being left exposed to public view for an hour and a half, owing to there being no hand ambulance available at Sankey. The, Coroner suggested that the Council should provide a hand ambu- lance for the removal of boglies. The Clerk, in reply to the Chairman, said on an average six to ten bellies were found in the canal at Sankey annually. Mr. Furness suggested that the Clerk should obtain information as to the cost of an ambu- lance, and this course was agreed to. There was a discussion about the village light- ing, and it was decided that the automatic system should be adopted all round.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.
COUNCIL REMINISCENCES.
Great Sankey Worthies Who Discussed Bygone Meetings.
A SMALL TURNOUT.

• Two meMbers of the Great Sankey Parish Council put in an appearance at the Council School on Monday night at the advertised time fixed for the holding of the annual meeting. They, however, could not get to business, owing to there not being a quorum, and some thirty- five minutes elapsed before the third member arrived. This was Mr. W. Furness, the chair- man of the Council.

-The. waiting period was n6tidlypet. as the two worthy councillors, with. theolerk; indulged jareniiniscences of old-timezparish'council meet- ings, when local parochial topics created .far more 'interest than they do nowadays, and, to -use 'Phrase of the tlerk.--taembers wont " whito in the face" during heated discussions. Those %days qzre :simply episodes:of the past, and a great change- has now come over the de- liberations of parish council meetings. As a rule, the meetings are brief and the business not of considerable importance. Such was the case at Mondak night's meeting of the Sankey Council. The first business to be decided was the elec-
tion of a chairman for the ensuing year, and one member suggested that they "should go on as before." namely, that Mr. Furness should continue in the office.

Thia,waa agreed to, and Mr. Furness;,retuxn- ing thanks, took the opportunity of. than4fing the Council 'llfor•thec kind '..assistance and 'co- operation:llW had always received. They had been ale to do some useful work for the par,ish: Their primary object and considerA4Mi>l4 been a minimum charge upon the rat;:iiiidlie was glad to say that charge had been almost nil. They had had the interest and the welfare of the ratepayers at heart Mr. J. G. Pownall was re-elected vice-chair- man, and Messrs. W. Ireland and R. Wright were re-appointed overseers. The other re-ap- pointments made were: The Rev. J. R. Jones, representative on the Education Sub-committee at Earlestown; and Messrs. S. Fair and A. Lowe as trustees of the Dutton's Charity.

div.head: CORONER AND A SCANDAL.
div.p: CORONER AND A SCANDAL.
FOR WAR HARDSHIPS.

Ten parishioners attended the annual parish meeting which followed. The principal busi- ness discussed was in relation to the work of the War Fund Committee, and Mr. Littler (treasurer) said ,that between. £7O and £BO had, been realised, in thel,v;illage. • • It'.was decided that:the War Fund Committee should call a meeting at an early date to dis- cuss whether anything else could be arranged in order to raise additional funds. Four-fifths of the money raised, it was ex- plained, had been forwarded direct to the Prince of Wales' Fund, the remaining portion being retained to meet local eases. The meeting passed a • resolution empowering the War Fund Committee to deal with the whole a the money raised- in the future, if it is thought necessary, for local and district pur- poses.

div.head: . PENKETH.
div.p: . PENKETH.

Private E. W.' Hughes In Hospital.—Private E. W. Hughes has written to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. William Hughes, Station-road, Pen- keth, explaining that he is in Lincoln Hos- pital, suffering from a broken shoulder-bone, sustained at the Front. The injury is progres- sing very favourably. The conditions are very comfortable, with the best of. food and atten- tion; also he is able to walk into the town every afternoon. The bane is set'. again. Private Ernest Hughes, of the A.S.C. Motor .Transport, was at one time employed, at the Tannery. Works, .afterwards taking up 'chauffeuring.

Wes!eyan Anniversary.—On'Sunday the Wes- leyau Chapel anniversary sermons were preached by the Rev. F. W. Kerniek, a former and much-appreciated minister of this circuit. Good congregations attended both the morning and evening services, as well as the special one held in the afternoon, when the chapel choir, under the leadership of Mr. George Carman, gave a• sacred cantata entitled "From Cross to Crown." Mr. A. W. Clatworthy presided at the organ. Mrs. J. G. Withinshaw, in the chair, made original suggestions in her introductor3 speech. The collections for the day, for which a special appeal was made, amounted to £43. On the following evening a highly interesting lecture was given in the schoolroom by the Rev. F. W. Kernick on "The Spirit of France." A good attendance showed the appreciation of the subject under consideration. Mr. C. E. Parker was,thairman. ,

div.head: BARN ABLAZE.
div.p: BARN ABLAZE.
Arson Charge Against young Man
Who-Has-Wandered.

A respectable looking man named Samuel Harold Kemp (22), but no fixed abode, was at the Warrington Occasional Court on Wednesday remanded for a week on a charge of maliciously setting fire to some barn buildings, the property of Peter Boardman, Lyon's Yam, penketh. The fire is estimated Co have- dOne damage. - It appears that the farm is managed by Mrs. Manning, and on Tuesday night a young man iiho was proceeding towards Sankey about 7.20 ' notioecl,a fire 'in a,large Dutch barn on the farm. Asjie*alted he Saw the prisoner, Kemp, walk quickly away- from the barn towards a gate. ' Another man who was cycling, appeared on the scene, and Considering prisoner's actions some- what suspicious, they kept him under observa- tion. They followed prisoner, whom they found standing near to the barn and the fire, but making no attempt to put the fire out. When questioned by one of the men as to why he had set fire to the stack ho made no reply. The .alarm was.given and the occupier of the farm appeared. 'The. men deelined to let prisoner go. and on P.C. Hopson arriving he was handed over to him. The officer 'had seen prisoner loitering about the village during the afternoon. The accused said "I struck a match, threw it among the stray, and put my foot on it?' Tired of Living.

The officer took prisoner into custody and 11,2 said "lam fed. up.,.! am tired of living, and Itotr7t care what: becomes of me' • Searched at the Tolice Station, he had ,two boxes of matches, cigarettes, one partially burned in his possession. Charged with setting fire to the farm buildings, accused replied, "Where did you get the proof from that I set it on fire. I will speak.for my- -k Alf.. in Court-

The police superintendent', in asking for a remand Of a week, said it was desirable that in. quiries should be made respecting accused, who. he said, had been a wanderer since he was 16 years of age..

div.head: FIRE BRIGADE AT WORK.
div.p: THE FIRE BRIGADE AT WORK.

About 7.30 p.m. on Tuesday information was received at Warrington by telephone that the fire broken out. A steam fire engine, in charge of Deputy-Supt. Cook, with a complement of men, was dispatched. On their arrival they found about forty tons of baled straw and twenty tons of hay on fire, under a corrugated iron shed_ The brigade quickly got to work. There were ple!city of willing assistants to help in turning over the debris. ' 'Tht, shed was not badly .damaged, : but the produce suffered badly. The loss is covered by insurance.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Boy Scouts.—This movement in connection with the Patlgato Wesleyan Sunday School is making rapid progress in the village. In a few weeks the membership has increased consider- ably, and -now the troop contains about 24 mem- bers. The boys are looking forward to a good time this Easter, as arrangements are being made for camping out in a barn at Radley Common, Houghton Green, which has been kindly; lent for the purpose by Mrs. Stanier. For some weeks' the boys have been hard at work clearing out the barn and making it ready for occupation, and, given fine weather, the first " camp " ought to be a huge success.

Parish Counsit—The annual Parish Council • meeting was held on Wednesday evening in. the C.E. Schools, Padgate, presided over by Mr. Geo. WaLker, supported by Messrs. Denham, Howard, Brimelow, Lythgoe and W. Potter. The election of officers took place, and Mr. W. S. Howard was appointed chairman for the ensuing year, with Mr. Brimeiow as vice-chairman. The overseers . (Messrs. Denham, Walker and Potter) were also re-elected. Mr. Geo. Mather was proposed as representative of the Parish Council on the Lancashire- Education Committee, Area 30, sit- ting at Earlegtown, and Mr. W. S. Howard was appointed Parish Council manager of Padgate C.E. School. A lengthy discussion took place with reference to the dust nuisance on Man- chester-road, and it was decided to send a strong representation to the Council to see if some- thing could not be done to remedy it. A fur- ther discussion took place regarding the presence of rats, motes and sparrows in the village, but it was decided that there was no necessity to levy a special rate to cover the destruction of these pests, as the distriot was practically free from them, at any rate in quantity.

div.head: INTERMEDIATE LEAGUE.
div.p: INTERMEDIATE LEAGUE.
Rylands's Brilliant Victory.
GREAT SURPRISE FOR HEATIIIDE • AT WILDERSPOOL.

Very disappointing indeed was, the, display 'giren. by, ,Heathside in their ncOunter • with Rylands's, at Wilderspool, on Saturday. The latter team were ..superior in all departments, and no one would attempt to deny them Of their nineteen points to nil victory, for it was only for ! about ten minutes in the first half that Heath- ' side were in the Rylands's quarters for any ;length of time, and during that time Me defence held good. . The game—a semi-final tie—was witnessed by a large and enthusiastic crowd, the majority of whom, judging by their conversations 'before .the ,qommeuemput of the match, thought it WOUld be an "easy thing for Heatbside',' (if. 'course, such views were quite natural, for Heath- side possess some brilliant backs—a ,department of their. team which has been the chief factor in gathering in VII points—a greater number pf paints than any :..other teaniin the League. , Consequently, great things were expected of them, and as they stepped on to the field, cries such as "Here's the lucky lads," and "Here's the winning team" greeted them.

Heath-side won the'. toss and elect&l to play with a strong sun and slight breeze at their backs. Bylands's started, and the first scrim- mage was formed at liaWway, from which itylands's broke away, but were penalised for off- side. From elie kick, Archer was tackled in possession, and, a minute later, he had a kick 'charged down by Foster just near the line, but the ball rolled dead. From the restart, Gleave put in a kick, and Archer received and made a fine run, during which he beat several opponents and removed play to half-way. Rylands'S .were, however:, penalised, and a good kick found touch. Frorothe scrimniage Lingard made a fine effort to 'break through, but the tack- ling was deadly. The ball became loose, and Britton endeavoured to clear from .off his own line, but his kick was charged down, and again the ball relied dead. , A.•l4tle later still.another -Ida, this time by Archer, , wwi-,chaigo, down, and again the ball rolled into touch.-- Foster now tried to get through, but was tackled.. A minute later Rylands's were awarded a free kick, but Harter failed. From the restart itylands's came away .A promising movement was spoiled by a knock on, and a minute later. Heathside broke away and forced the Rylands's full-back to. kick: dead. Archer having kicked over his own line, t five yards scrum was ordered,- and for an 'infringe- ment by a Heathside forward, Rylands's were awarded a free-kick, by means of which play was removed to half-way. Shortly afterwar.is they were awarded another free-kick for obstrue- lion.- and play was thus removed to the vicinity of the Heathside goal-stumps. Here the Rylands's forwards joined wholeheartedly in a movement which ended in Savory going ore: under the sticks, .Dumbell kicking a goal. This ~was-.after 25 -rniniites' -play, and 'came as a rare eye-opener.

_ Roused by this reverse, Heathside came away with a tremendous rusb, but Rylands's tackling was deadly. Dale (Heathside) and Savory (Rylands's) now became engaged in a display of ,fistieuffs,' with the result that Referee Bibby derecr..thern from the' field. Having been awarded a free-kick for obstruction, Rylands's tried for goal, but the kick was a miserable failure. •
lialf-timo:—llylands's, 5 points; Hedthside. nil.
Tries Galore.

Heatbside commenced .the second half, but Rylands's were the first to attack. Griffiths, the Heathside full-back—and, by the way, their best player—drove them back, but llylands's came again by means of short rushes. They were, however, again driven back, and when in a favourable position, Heathside were awarded a free-kick, but Harter failed miserably.
