div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN MISS SEVERAL CHANCES.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN MISS SEVERAL CHANCES.
But ,Win Comfortably.

The. return, match -on Saturday- between rington and Hyde resulted in the Warring- toniana atoning for the -previous week's defeat at Hyde, and although victory was claimed by the odd gaal in three, there could be no two opinions as to the better side. The Warrington Club deserved their victory, but the score, 2-1, in their favour, does not give-the correct im- pression of the relative merits of the two teams, in fact, Hyde should consider themselves lucky that they were not defeated by five or six goals to one. •

Warrington had themselves to blame for the narrowness- 'of their win, and the ineptness.of the forwards to take advantage of the oppor7; tunities ,prOented them was one of the remark- able features of the game Missed .chanei,s‘," predominated the Whole ninky minutes; horn the spectators' point of view the match was dis- appointing, for nothing more thwarts thP enthusiasm •of a. football crowd; than to see a sequence of "misses." The spectators, how- ever, had this satisfaction—Warrington won.

Warrington fielded a strong side, while Hyde rearranged their forward line, but it was not as' successful from a scoring and playing point of view as on the previous Saturday. They were poor in comparison.

Warrington were the far superior side, and had most of the play. At times the forwards showed capital 'combination, Whitfield. keeo.7lg his wing men well supplied with passes; and, they, in turn, doing their bit satisfactorily. But it was in the Hyde goal area that the for- wards failed to force home the several useful chances that came to them. Certainly the ball was :a bit.lively, but the chief faultlay with the Warrington 'folarc's,' because coal not shoot straight and put some sting into their shots. Another essential for goal.-seoring —steadiness--in front of --goal. was entirely absent.

On Saturday's form it is difficult to under- stand how Hyde, the previons ,acelp notched th goals. it may be they left their shooting-bos behind. During the whole ninety. minutes, the ITyde• forwurds4 never gave the least aupression that they were goal-getters. The only goal credited to them was a gift.

The game on a whole was a scrappy one, neither side showing -anything like- good-foot, ball. • What few brilliant flashe,s there 'Were came from the •Warrington team, and JZe-asion- ally the crowd would get enthusiastic. There was a lack of the go-ahead tpirit,in the-move- ments of both teams.; , ‘:

The first half was only moderately e.,lnt'ested, and. though Warrington had the 'bait ol the ex- changes they could not penetrate the Hyde goal. The ..forwards Worked several good opbnings, but they could ppt..p* .on, tho finishing:P.oth, be- 'Cause they laeked'initiative and sholtlit;',..power:. The Hyde defence had a lot of work to-do, and managed to keep their goal. intact- until close upon hall-time. Warrington took the lead as the result of a, .gpod forward effort, Whitfiold notching a long delayed goal.

But this suecesB was short lived. Hyde had a spell of attacking, and Kite allowing a shot to slip through his Ilancls•into the net, put Hyde on level terms. It W 11,4 a bad blunder, and enabled Hyde to be on level terms at the inter- val.

The second half opened with a certain amount of liveliness on the part of the Warringtonians, and the forwards seemeed bent on getting goals this half. Play had only been in progress a few minutes when Warrington got their second goal, Foster putting the tinishlng touch on a big eilort made by Owen. .Following this success, ,the Hyde goal -was subjected to hea;t; pressure, and had sortie narrow escapes. Had the Warrington vanguard eNercised a little better judgment in. Making the best use, of. the openings presented they 'would have piled on a few goals. Most of\ the pay was in the 11.,y,!! quarters, and Butterworth in goal inade.serne smart save.-,. Warrington tailed t aild more goals, and the game ended u ith Hyde mill beaten on. the run:of pl4Ly, but not fioni the ,NIIA of 'gcial s4:oring.

Warrington,vero smartor in all ,department; than Hyde. Kite is undoubtedly. off form just now, and he was none too Safe in goal. cook- son_and Leah were two capable backs and. never gave the llyde forwards room to shine. .Broster, Worrall and Haywood in the half-back line. accomplished good- work; While of the forwards,' Foster and Whitfield were always prominent, if not altogether sueccsful in their shooting. •

Worrall, a centrclhalf of local reputation. has ,played many . games ;on the Lovely-lane ground when he was a aneuiber of the We/Itield team, , and he also Tendered good sqvice to CroAfield'a Works' foam, both in the North Cheshire League and in the Works' CoMPett= Hon. mi is a member of the Warrington Terri- torkals, and only eempleted.his term of engage- ment a week or two age. So satisfactory was his display that the Town committee should have no doubts of giving him an extenderi trial. The following players. turned out:—

Allen is a local lad,'whO liak'griYed for Oswestry United.; The committee have omitted Broster and 'Gee from the team on Account Of them being engaged on munitions and notwishing.-tkern- to lose tizne-at- work.

div.head: MOTRALL TAX.
div.p: MOTRALL TAX.
The Sport Is Willing To ft Its " Hit."

There will be a unique gathering of football officials at the offices of the Football Association on 'Tuesday next, writes "The Veteran," in the "Daily Dispatch." 'Deputations of three codes will be in conference with a representative ot the Treasury in respect .to • the working .of the amusement tax: in retation!.tolootball.,.Offiial representing the Football Association, the Rugby Union, and the Northern Union will be present. The Northern Union have held a meeting at the Grosvenor Hotel, • Manchester, to discuss the matter. They appointed IltioArs. -J. •H. Smith, J. B. Cooke and. J. Platt .to represent them at the conference in • London. Many in- teresting points, I understand, are to be dis- cussed, and one thing is certain—that the foot- ball representati'ves, knowing how willing the sport is to do its bit in the matter, will be only too anions to help. the Ocrvernnient- the best way they can. War conditions have created nianY interesting situations in the football world. Last week we had Northern Union and Rugby Union Men playing side' by - side at Headingley• for the sacred cause' of charity; both the. Association and the Rugby game have done.. a noble work in the same direction, and now, next week shall 'have representatives, Of „three., distinct bodies • in' eonferenee- working oxit' a 'same whieh will help , pay .for :war. :...Sport •••im• the future will .be all. the better far the,e happy reunions. •

MILITARY TRIBUNAL.
Licensed Victualler Who Distrusts Barmen.
APPRENTICE'S INDENTURES.
The business at the Warrington •Tribun4l yesterday afternoon . was .of a very dull char- acter, and the only • interesting-. point Avas. licensed victualler's candid opinion about bar-

men. . The publican in enestion appealed for the exemption of his son,, who, he said, assisted in the bar and looked .after the house generally. He was indispensable to the carrying on of the business. Captain Mathams : Do you employ anyone else P—No. • . Is there any reason why you "should not employ a man over military age?—l would give the place up first. • For sentimental reasons P—Tl4, veasons are you cannot get honest people. It will be a losS. to you 6-give up the hduse? —lt will; my living will be gone. Do. you, suggest it is impossible to get an honest barman P—lt think it is. . Applieant asked Captain Mathams to tellhirn a house in-the-town where a.•:•Stranger was put, in charge, and Captain Mathains' said he knew. nothing about the houses In Warrington. • • Captain Mathams : Who is dishonest—the . public or the publicartF—l don't know. Appellant added that .he had: gone throUgh it, and knew what he was talking• about. • % The Tribunal granted temporary exemption. till May 31st, and informed appellant that' he could apply again. . TYPICAL CASES OF CONDITIONAL EXEMPTION. A painter and decorator, the sole support of his widowed mother, was granted exemption till July 14th. , Messrs. James Fairclough and Sons, millers, applied for the exemption of four employes, a millwright hand,' a steam engine driver, a clerk and a traveller. . The two former were given conditional ex-, emption, the appeal of the -clerk was refused, and the traveller was exempted till. May 31st; the Tribunal 'expressing the hope that the firm would obtain someone else to fill his place. An insurance agent, married, was put back a month in order.to allow.. him satisfactorily to arrange his business affairs; • • , '• ,:2 • Three employes of the Peroxide Company' were granted conditional 'exemption. .- • • - Mr.: Steel 'applied on behalf of the United Velvet Cutters' Association for the exemption. of a tooler, and it was stated that 'BO per cent.. of the trade was export. It was impossible 'to replace the man, and. if he had to go Some .43 females would be thrown idle: They' had pro- vided motor power ta take the place of foot power, for one of their employes who had lost I his right leg in the war.--Conditional exemption I was granted. A scrap iron and -rag dealer, married, was ' granted exemption till 'May 31st. . An appeal was made on behalf of a young man • who had not completed his indentures; The father of the young 'man said he was un:' able to get ',the indentures produced at the Tribunal. and the Chairman (Dr. 'Joseph) thought they had a right to 'see the indentures. Alderman Tinnion jocularly suggested that a corporal and two privates should be. dispatched for the indentures, and brought on the'point of the bayonet. . . . A •"sergeant: was detailed off to see the ,inden- tures,. end • when he returned he informed 'the' Tribunal of the date of the signing of the indentures and • the • date when completed. • The Tribunal was satisfied and granted 'con- ditional exemption. • Messrs. Armitage and Rigby had conditional exemption granted to two of their workmen, and three months" exemption to a third, • The firm withdrew an appeal in the case Of another workman who had declined to attend work regularly: It was stated . that- 33 one of 54 men of military age had enlisted since the war began. They had only five labourers, and they were so hard pushed that the men worked 70 and 80 hours per week.

div.head: SOCIALIST'S FLIGHT TO SCOTLAND.
div.p: SOCIALIST'S FLIGHT TO SCOTLAND.
Police Court Sequel.

Three conscientious objectors—two of whom absconded. to the hills of Scotland, to use a phrase of the Chief Constable's—were placed in the dock at the Borough Court on Thursday, and charged with failing to report themselves under the Military Service Act. Considerable public interest was manifested in the proceedings. The accused were Thomas Howard, a well-known Socialist, 3, Frederick- street; Harold Gough Brandwood, furniture salesman, 26; Percy-street; :and Own Owen, a boxmaker; of 34, Pinner's Brow.

div.head: MILK. AND • HONEY Irk SCOTLAND'S
div.p: MILK. AND • HONEY Irk SCOTLAND'S

Respecting ,Howard, the Chief Constable said the Magistrates might have observe d .from. time to time the appeal of - a windew cleaner which • appeared in the local Press. Prisoner .first appeared before the local. Tribunal to be exempted from Military service,, but ;the appli- cation ,was refused. He took his appeal to the Liyerpoel Tribunal, but it was again refused, and he then entered another appeal at the Lond.on.Tribunal, but was not considered. A nOtiee Niras posted to accused by the military authorities to ,report himself on April Prisoner absconded from Warrington, and went to the Scotch hills to live on milk and honey. He was found in the vicinity .of Ayr, and was brought to Orford Barracks under military escort. Colonel Meggridge handed him ,over to , Colonel Mocatta. 1 Continuing, the Chief Constable said there was interesting reading in the case. as a result lof prisoner's application before the Tribunal 'He said it would be a , grave violation of his conscience if he participated in .any,.movement which he belieVed was against the 'best, the highest.' and noblest ideals of humanity. When arrested- he made some statement, to the officer that he .ha &gots a discharge from His Majesty's Forces.' That discharge had never been dig, closed before the Tribunal when the case was considered. Even if. he had belonged to an "old volunteer detachment and had been discharged. that was no excuse that he should be exempted from militarV service. So far he had nut the military authorities to the PYCIDOTIFR of 2.5 or ga in bringing him from the hills of Scotland.

div.head: “AN ABSOLUTE ANSWER.”
div.p: “AN ABSOLUTE ANSWER.”

Mr. Risque, of Manchester, appeared for Howard. who, be said, had an absolute answer to the charge. He was instructing counsel for accused, and he accordingly applied for an adjournment. The Chief Constable said neither he nor the military authorities objected to an adjourn- ment. There was, however, no reason why there should be delay, and he suggested that the case should come before the same magistrates, if adjourned. Mr. Risque said it was necessary to obtain evidence. He applied for bail for the accused. The Chief Constable opposed,:and said Howard absconded, and had admitted screening himself by getting among the Scotch hills. The ease was adjourned till Wednesday, bail beipg rd used. Later Mr. Risque applied for permission to allow the Rey. H. T. Dixon, Messrs. A. Seabury and J. Harris to interview Howard. The Chief Constable said he had no objection to the reverend gentleman interviewing Howard, but he did not want interviews to be granted ad libitum. The Court granted permission 13RANDWOOD FINED £5.

When Harold Gough Brandwood was charged the Chief Constable said he was arrested by the Ayrshire Constabulary. A notice was posted to accused calling upon him to report on April Bth. Prior to receiving the notice, he made application for exemption to the local Tribunal, which was dismissed. He then appealed to the Liverpool Tribunal, who placed him in non- combatant service. An escort was sent to 'Ayr- Shire to bring accused back, and he asked the Bench to pay regard to the amount of momi it cost to bring him to W,arringten. ,-Acc'used-said he, went away to aVoid. div.head: MR. J. A. RANSOME INTERVENES.
div.p: MR. J. A. RANSOME INTERVENES.
Court Scene.

Mr. J. A. Ransom°. a Cheshire m4,istrate, figured prominently in a case at the Borough Court on Friday, when Fred Broadhurst, joiner, of 89, Marsh House-lane, was charged with fail- ing to report himself under the Military Service Act on April Bth.

' Detective Turner said he received, information from the military authorities that aCCUSed had :not reported himself, and on Thursday' after- noon he visited the .Cheshire Lines, Waggon Works at Warrington... He Saw 'accused and asked him why he had not reported himself to the military 'authorities, and he replied that-he had appealed to the local and the Liverpool tribunals on conscientious grounds, gut had been refused. lie said he was in possession of a badge given him by the railway company. Witness told him that a- letter had been re- ceived from the Cheshire Lines manager stating that accused had received instructions to report himself.

Accused said he had a war badge and certifi- cate, which he understood when withdrawn from him, allowed him two months' exemption under the Military Service Act. lie wished to claim two months' exemption from that day. The Chief Constable said the accused had been told to enlist by the Cheshire Lines manager, but he wanted to) screen himself, like many others, behind the war badge. Accused and many other men were making it as awk- ward as possible for the authorities, and people in better stations of life were assisting such men to avoid military service. Accused had been released by the company so that he could join the Army. - A gentleman, who was in the body of Ma Court, then stood up and asked for an adjourn- ment of the case. . .

' The Chid Constable: You have no right to appear before the Court. It is a highly im- proper course of procedure. The Chairman (Mr. S. Wright): What is your name? The gentleman in question said his name was Ransome. The Chairman: What connectiofl is there be- tween this man and you? Mr. Ransome: lie is not a relation of mine.

The Chairman: Is he in your employ P---No, Sir. There has been no time to obtain a solicitor to appear 6rt this 'man's behalf. The Chief Constable: There has been plenty of time. He has been in custody since Thurs- day. Every effort is being made to thwart justice being carried but. Mr. Ransom° : We have had no opportunitY.

_ The -Chairman': We cannot give you that opportunity here.' We cannot listen to any- thing you have to say. The Chief Constable said if he wanted advice he could have consulted his solicitor. There was no jtistificatien to, ask .for artadjourninent. It vrtis a most improper course for a magistrate to come into that court and take it upon him- self to ask for a remand.
--Accused was fined 405., and ordered to b- handed over to the military authorities.

div.head: THOUGHT HE WAS INDISPENSABLE.
div.p: THOUGHT HE WAS INDISPENSABLE.

Thomas Wilson, painter, 32, Norris-street, was charged with failing to report himself to the military authorities on April Bth. Detective Green gave evidencei to arresting accused on Thursday. .Asked why he had not 'reported. himself he reftea, " I hate got -a war badge from the Cheshire • Lines Company. Accused informed the Court that he thought he was indispensable. As a Member of St. John Ambulance Brigade lie was mobilised in August, 1914, and the company. refused' him his release because he understood he was indispensable. Accused ',Was. fined 40s. and Aiando over to the military 'authorities.

div.p: ENGAGED ON WAR WORK.

The difficulty in getting 'men was abnormal, awl without water proofers it would be impossible to turn out goods for the Army'and Navy. They had done their best to supplement men by female Tabour. A well-built farth hand,. named Percy Bam- ford; of -Rixton, appealed at Liverpool. on Monday. His parents and .his grandparents on both sides were .said JO have been of the same religious Persuasion. '•:Questioned as to whether•threChristadelphian.s- -• had ever opposed : any otixer:' war than this, he said that they took :their. nam,e.at, the time of the American Civil War, ..and they claimed, •• and were •granted, exemption from service with both the.FederalS and the Confederates. The Lord Mayor: Are we to understand that you receive .the benefits of soeiety, but are not willing to give anything in return am willing , to 'do anything I canto help' the !country, but • I am not prepared to •take any part with the r.iiliiary. • ! The pro- phetic writings point to the -fact that Britain would be the winufv. , •

Bamford did not appeal himself, but was appealed for by gentleman who has previopsly taken an interest in the Christadelphian ob- jectors. Tllfuneral took place on. Thursday afternoon. At the doe an ienasit.o Russian anthein, " Give Him Rest; 0 Christ"- was beautifully sung by the choir. Frank Johnson, one of the, five z'oldier-sons of Mr. and Mrs. 'Johnson, 17, Stain- forti-street,. is unofficially reported killed in action ' • Writing to Miss Johnson, Lieutenant E. C. K.
